Name: The Bony Fish Fossils of the Western Limfjord – Evolution and Climate Adaptation in the Earliest Eocene

Short Description: The serial property, located in the Western Limfjord sea of northern Jutland, Denmark, comprise the coastal cliffs of Hanklit and Knudeklint, which contain some of the world’s best-preserved fossil fishes. The property represents the oldest and most important site for understanding the early evolution and diversification of modern bony fishes (teleosts) following the end-Cretaceous mass extinction. Preserved within diatomite-rich deposits and volcanic ash layers, the exceptional fossil record spans the Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum (PETM) and the subsequent cooling period, providing unique evidence of biotic responses to major climatic change. The property contains abundant and exceptionally well-preserved marine and terrestrial fossils, including fishes, sea turtles, birds, insects, plants, and microfossils, offering an unparalleled insight into the earliest Eocene biosphere. It preserves between 25 and 29 fish orders and more than 80 fish species, documenting the evolution and adaptation of early modern fish lineages during a period of rapid environmental change.

Description: The serial property, located in the Western Limfjord sea of northern Jutland, Denmark, comprise the coastal cliffs of Hanklit and Knudeklint, which contain some of the world’s best-preserved fossil fishes. The property represents the oldest and most important site for understanding the early evolution and diversification of modern bony fishes (teleosts) following the end-Cretaceous mass extinction. Preserved within diatomite-rich deposits and volcanic ash layers, the exceptional fossil record spans the Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum (PETM) and the subsequent cooling period, providing unique evidence of biotic responses to major climatic change. The property contains abundant and exceptionally well-preserved marine and terrestrial fossils, including fishes, sea turtles, birds, insects, plants, and microfossils, offering an unparalleled insight into the earliest Eocene biosphere. It preserves between 25 and 29 fish orders and more than 80 fish species, documenting the evolution and adaptation of early modern fish lineages during a period of rapid environmental change.

Justification: Brief synthesis The Bony Fish Fossils of the Western Limfjord – Evolution and Climate Adaptation in the Earliest Eocene represent the world’s single best fossil site to illustrate the evolution of the earliest modern fishes of the Eocene epoch that followed shortly after the mass extinction at the end of the Cretaceous. Located in the Western Limfjord sea of northern Jutland, Denmark, the serial property comprises the two largest and best coastal cliffs that contain some of the best-preserved fossil fishes in the world and that represent the only known fish-bearing succession that covers the very warm climatic conditions of the Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum (PETM) and the immediately succeeding cooler period. The property comprising the coastal cliffs of Hanklit and Knudeklint, located on the islands of Mors and Fur, respectively, is protected as a pristine reference for fossils in their characteristic source of diatomite-rich Fur Formation and Stolleklint Clay with volcanic ash layers. The ash layers and glaciotectonic structures are important supporting features for correlation, dating and interpretation. Fossil discoveries continue to be made in open excavations and in cliff debris as well as in nearby mo-clay pits with which the museums have close collaboration. Exceptional fossils include marine organisms such as fishes, sea-turtles, diatoms, silicoflagellates and dinoflagellates, together with several invertebrate groups, and terrestrial organisms such as nearly complete bird skeletons, abundant insects, spores and pollen, together with rarer leaves and petrified tree trunks. Criterion (viii): The property constitutes the world’s oldest and single best site for the study of the early evolution of modern bony fish lineages (teleosts), shortly after the fifth and last mass extinction of life at the end of the Cretaceous. Overall, it offers a supreme insight in the earliest Eocene biosphere because it contains abundant and diverse, extremely well-preserved fossils from both oceanic and continental environments, and because it is the only known substantial teleost-bearing site which documents the biotic response to one of the most significant temperature fluctuations in the Earth’s history – the Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum (PETM). The attributes of Outstanding Universal Value comprise the fish fossils documenting early ‘modern’ fish evolution and diversification; the biotic and geochemical record across the PETM and the succeeding recovery phase expressed in the Stolleklint Clay and lower Fur Formation; and the diverse marine and terrestrial fossil assemblages that provide an exceptional insight into the earliest Eocene biosphere. Abundant, diverse, and outstandingly well-preserved fossils provide an unparalleled insight into the origin of the earliest ancestors of many modern organisms, together with their early evolution. This is the oldest known (c. 56 to 54.6 Ma), exceptionally well-preserved occurrence of ray-finned fish lineages that emerged succeeding the Cretaceous-Paleogene mass extinction. The property presents between 25 and 29 fish orders and more than 80 species that underwent significant changes in response to rapid climate change. Integrity The property is the largest, most intact, and accessible, fossil site that is fully representative of the Western Limfjord deposits. It encompasses all palaeontological and palaeoclimate change-related attributes within a natural environment integrated into a protected area network. There are no adverse effects of development and/or neglect, and the property is not under threat. Some impact through natural cliff erosion may be accelerated by climate change in the long-term, although no major conservation challenges are envisaged for the foreseeable future. Fossil discoveries continue to be made in mo-clay pits in the wider setting. This is seen as an advantage since palaeontology is an extractive science that involves the removal of fossils for research. The two regional museums have close collaboration with industry in terms of access for research, and popular fossil collecting, without impacting the property. Protection and management requirements The principal protection and management requirement is to ensure that the cliff exposures, fossil recovery, collection protocols and regulation of visitor access enable the long-term conservation of the attributes of Outstanding Universal Value over time. Site management needs to ensure coordinated cliff-exposure stewardship, clear protocols for fossil discovery, reporting and curation as well as research access, monitoring of coastal processes and site condition, and practical provisions for safe visitor access within carrying capacities, interpretation and education. Adaptive approaches are maintained in response to any future increases in visitation or climate-related coastal change. The property, acknowledged for its significant national and international geological value, is afforded the highest level of protection under Danish law through a robust and comprehensive legal framework, giving the two component parts top priority in the planning procedures of local governments. Key legislation includes the Nature Protection Act, the Shore Protection Zone provisions, the Planning Act, the Museum Act, and the Danekræ system. Danekræ is defined as earth-found, nature-made objects of exceptional or unique natural scientific and/or exhibition value. Other applicable national instruments include the Raw Materials Act and apply to both component parts. No commercial extraction of mo-clay is possible in the property. A collaborative management organisation is anchored at the local level on the two municipalities and their respective museums, supported by landowners, local communities, and state authorities. The management plan defines the management system of the property. Overall, the protection context is strengthened by the long-standing involvement of museums and research institutions that curate collections, support documentation, and provide an institutional pathway for reporting, safeguarding and scientific use of specimens.

Natural Criteria: n8

Name: Aalto Works

Short Description: The property consists of thirteen modern buildings and ensembles across Finland (1928–1988) that exemplify the 20th‑century Modern Movement and its response to broad social needs. These civic, community, and residential structures—found in both urban and rural settings—are internationally associated with Alvar Aalto, yet they reflect the collaborative creativity of Aalto, Aino Marsio‑Aalto, Elissa Aalto, the Aalto studio, and their design partners. Rooted in Finnish building traditions while drawing on global modernist ideas, the works express a human‑centred, site‑specific, and empathetic vision that distinguishes Finland’s contribution to modern architecture.

Description: The property consists of thirteen modern buildings and ensembles across Finland (1928–1988) that exemplify the 20th‑century Modern Movement and its response to broad social needs. These civic, community, and residential structures—found in both urban and rural settings—are internationally associated with Alvar Aalto, yet they reflect the collaborative creativity of Aalto, Aino Marsio‑Aalto, Elissa Aalto, the Aalto studio, and their design partners. Rooted in Finnish building traditions while drawing on global modernist ideas, the works express a human‑centred, site‑specific, and empathetic vision that distinguishes Finland’s contribution to modern architecture.

Justification: Brief synthesis The Aalto Works comprise thirteen modern buildings and building ensembles designed between 1928 and 1988 by Alvar Aalto in collaboration with his first spouse Aino Marsio-Aalto and second spouse Elissa Aalto, as well as the employees of the Aalto studio (1923-1994) and Artek (founded 1935), their affiliated interior design and furnishings company. Located in both urban and rural areas of Finland, the serial property bears witness to the application of global principles of the 20th-century Modern Movement, as a response to new societal and universal needs. Strongly rooted in local building traditions, the Aalto Works are characterised by a comprehensive and individualistic design approach driven by an empathetic, site-specific, and human-centred vision, where each project is unique and responds to specific programmatic requirements. The serial property showcases the Aaltos’ experiments in construction technology, architectural aesthetics, spatial sequences, lighting, and the use of both natural and industrial materials. Each building is carefully integrated into its surroundings. This synthetic design approach also encompassed interior design, merging industrial elements with local traditional materials. Most of the buildings still feature their original collections of furniture and lighting designed by the Aalto studio. Criterion (ii): Through an organic functionalist approach, the Aalto Works adapted global Modern Movement ideas to local contexts, seamlessly integrating exteriors with interiors and harmonising with their settings. This architecture offers an outstanding response to universal societal needs, prioritising citizen well-being throughout the modernisation process. By bridging modern concepts with building traditions, the collective design approach introduced a new language of form, materiality, and production methods, executed with exceptional sensitivity, simplicity, and integrity. Integrity The serial property contains all the necessary attributes that convey its Outstanding Universal Value, including structures, features, and spaces created by the Aalto studio. These elements best illustrate the integration of a new international architectural language with traditional local ideas, driving the modernisation of the 20th-century society through a sensitive, human-centred approach to architecture and design. All component parts are in a good state of conservation. They remain largely unchanged since construction and, in the majority of cases, retain their original relationship with their associated landscapes and settings. Most interiors still feature significant original fittings and furniture. Furthermore, many buildings continue to serve their original purpose or have been adapted for sympathetic functions. None of the component parts currently suffer from the adverse effects of development or neglect. The Paimio Sanatorium (component part 02) is vulnerable in terms of ensuring its continued appropriate use and requires significant conservation efforts; however, measures have been put in place to mitigate potential losses. Authenticity The serial property demonstrates a high degree of authenticity, both as a whole and at the level of each component part. Conservation efforts and management of each component part have ensured that the authenticity of their forms and designs is sustained. A minimal-intervention approach and a firm commitment to preserving original materials and finishes have resulted in a remarkably high level of material authenticity across most component parts. In some instances, previous alterations that compromised design authenticity have been reversed through recent conservation projects. The majority of the buildings retain their original uses and functions, or have been converted for purposes compatible with their original purpose. All component parts remain in their original location, maintaining their relationships with their settings, landscape features, and significant views. Each component part has been thoroughly documented, researched, inventoried, and described in statutory and planning documents. The Alvar Aalto Archives serve as a vital resource for the ongoing understanding and stewardship of the serial property. Furthermore, the Alvar Aalto Foundation safeguards the material and intellectual legacy of the studio, providing expert assistance for the repair and maintenance of buildings and sites designed by the Aaltos. Protection and management requirements The legal protection of the property falls under several regulatory frameworks and all thirteen component parts have been granted legal protection under national laws. It is based primarily on the Act on the Protection of the Built Heritage (498/2010), the Land Use and Building Act (132/1999) separated into the Land Use Act and the Building Act in 2025, and the Church Act (1054/1993). It protects historic buildings and their fixed interiors, groups of buildings, and their surroundings of national significance while the land use regulations promote sustainable development and ensures public participation in planning through planning mechanisms, including zoning as well as impact assessments required in land-use and development processes. It also embraces measures to protect Built Cultural Heritage Sites of National Significance, including those under the World Heritage Convention. The Church Act protects the relevant ecclesiastical buildings, interiors and art. The management of the property combines existing and new arrangements and will be organised on two levels: at the local level, for the management of the individual component parts; and at the national level, for the management, coordination and supervision of the serial property as a whole. A coordinated management system will be established through the appointment of a site manager, a coordinating management body and thirteen local management bodies. The management, conservation and research activities relating to the property are facilitated by the work of the Finnish Heritage Agency as well as by the Alvar Aalto Foundation. The Aalto Works Management Plan was developed in a participatory process and provides management arrangements, identifies issues and sets management objectives for the series as a whole, and for each individual component part. Heritage Impact Assessment procedures are implemented for any project likely to have an impact on a protected national monument, including World Heritage properties.

Cultural Criteria: c2

Name: Beaches of the D-Day Landings, Normandy, 1944

Short Description: The serial property comprises six component parts along approximately 80 km of the Normandy coastline, encompassing Utah, Omaha, Gold, Juno, and Sword Beaches, as well as Pointe du Hoc. These sites are directly associated with the Allied landings of 6 June 1944, the opening phase of Operation Overlord, which marked the beginning of the liberation of Western Europe from Nazi occupation during the Second World War. The property preserves significant remains of the German Atlantic Wall, including casemates, artillery batteries, fire‑control posts, and resistance nests, alongside battlefield traces, original wartime equipment, and major commemorative landscapes such as the American Cemetery at Colleville‑sur‑Mer. Together, these elements form an exceptional cultural landscape shaped both by the events of 1944 and by their enduring remembrance.

Description: The serial property comprises six component parts along approximately 80 km of the Normandy coastline, encompassing Utah, Omaha, Gold, Juno, and Sword Beaches, as well as Pointe du Hoc. These sites are directly associated with the Allied landings of 6 June 1944, the opening phase of Operation Overlord, which marked the beginning of the liberation of Western Europe from Nazi occupation during the Second World War. The property preserves significant remains of the German Atlantic Wall, including casemates, artillery batteries, fire‑control posts, and resistance nests, alongside battlefield traces, original wartime equipment, and major commemorative landscapes such as the American Cemetery at Colleville‑sur‑Mer. Together, these elements form an exceptional cultural landscape shaped both by the events of 1944 and by their enduring remembrance.

Justification: Brief synthesis On 6 June 1944, Operation Neptune, the first phase of Operation Overlord, conceived to open a new Western European Front during the Second World War against the forces of the Third Reich, was launched from beaches on the Normandy coast that have come to be known as the Beaches of the D-Day Landings. Along with the military action and human sacrifice on multiple fronts in Eastern Europe, Northern Africa and the Pacific, the Normandy Landings was one of the decisive moments in the Second World War, when after years of planning, seventeen allied nations collaborated in military, logistical, political, and moral resources as part of a concerted plan to overcome a regime of conquest and genocide. The serial property, comprising six component parts, commemorates the way years of planning and alliance-building culminated in collective, multinational, logistical and military efforts that marked the beginning of the end of the Second World War in Western Europe, ultimately contributing to the toppling of a totalitarian regime and paving the way for reconstruction, reconciliation, and a renewed commitment to collective security. The Beaches of the D-Day Landings also embody, symbolise, and evoke memories of the immense human sacrifice made to begin to break the entrenched authoritarian regime of the Third Reich that occupied most of Europe in the mid-20th century. The landing operations, launched on 6 June 1944, took place on five beaches (from west to east): Utah Beach, Omaha Beach, Gold Beach, Juno Beach and Sword Beach, as well as at Pointe du Hoc, the sixth amphibious assault site, constituting altogether the component parts of the serial property. Each site still bears the traces of the event. The serial property contains many tangible attributes: the beaches themselves, the five landing sites of 6 June 1944, and an amphibious assault site; remains of the most remarkable structures illustrating the logistical efforts made to ensure the success of Operation Neptune, particularly the artificial harbour known as Mulberry B; remains of the defensive system or “Atlantic Wall” that the Allies faced; traces left by the confrontation in the landscape, deliberately preserved as a reminder of the event; memorial sites created since 1944; memorial monuments, and finally, the American Military Cemetery at Colleville-sur-Mer, built in the immediate vicinity of Omaha Beach. They also contain intangible attributes, memories of the event to which they are intrinsically linked, having acquired strong symbolic significance. In paying tribute to the victims of the confrontation, the Beaches of the D-Day Landings have also become a place of reconciliation between former belligerents. Criterion (vi): The Beaches of the D-Day Landings, Normandy, 1944 are a site of memory directly and materially associated with the event known as the “Normandy Landings”, which took place in 1944 during the Second World War. Operation Neptune, launched on 6 June 1944 on the Normandy coast, was the first phase of Operation Overlord, designed to open a new front in Western Europe against the troops of the Third Reich, one of the decisive moments in the Second World War, which marked the beginning of the end of the war in Western Europe. The Beaches of the D-Day Landings outstandingly and tangibly embody, symbolically commemorate and evoke memories of the concerted, multinational collaboration and coordination of logistical and military efforts, and the immense human sacrifice required to break an entrenched authoritarian occupation in Europe in the mid-20th century and paved the way for reconstruction, reconciliation, and a renewed commitment to collective security. Integrity The serial property includes all the component parts necessary to express its Outstanding Universal Value, particularly its associative value. The series incorporates the beaches themselves, as landing and amphibious assault sites on 6 June 1944; remains of the logistical facilities used for the offensive; remains of the defensive system or “Atlantic Wall” that the Allies faced; traces left by the confrontation in the landscape, deliberately preserved; commemorative sites; memorial monuments; and finally, a military cemetery that provides a representation of other military cemeteries. The individual integrity of each component part varies, but all nevertheless present a sufficient set of attributes to fully express the associative value of the serial property. The landscape integrity of the serial property, although vulnerable, can be described as satisfactory as it is adequately preserved despite pressures, including urban and tourism development on some component parts. Threats related to the natural evolution of the coastline and from facilities supporting the transition to renewable energy should also be closely monitored. Authenticity The serial property retains a set of attributes which authentically attest to the site of memory associated with the event known as the “Normandy Landings”. Historical knowledge of the context and course of the operation, as well as the defensive and offensive systems, is well established. This high level of knowledge contributes to the appreciation of the authenticity of the remains left behind by Operation Neptune on the beaches of Normandy. Most of the materials comprising the component parts have been affected, both by human intervention – in particular cleaning and the recovery of materials, which became unavoidable following the events – and by natural erosion. However, the remaining traces have been preserved without the need for any significant intervention to restore them. The defensive elements damaged by the fighting were deliberately preserved as they were. The authenticity of the immediate landscape setting is generally good, despite occasional alterations and some evolution due to natural and human factors. Overall, the tangible and intangible attributes of the serial property retain their ability to evoke memories of the scope and sacrifices of the confrontation, but they are vulnerable to the cumulative change that could impact on this ability. Protection and management requirements The entire perimeters of the serial property and its extensive buffer zone (comprising a maritime area and a terrestrial area) are protected by a wide range of measures, in particular under national legislation governed by the Heritage Code, the Environment Code and the Urban Planning Code, as well as the Littoral Law. Safeguarding and conservation of tangible and intangible attributes are also ensured by a diversity of administrative and protected-area mechanisms relating to heritage, nature, landscapes, or biodiversity, such as regulatory mechanisms (e.g. historic monuments or nature reserves); land acquisition; contractual protection (e.g. Natura 2000); and international conventions (e.g. Ramsar Convention). In addition, the maritime portion of the property, located on the foreshore and in the territorial waters, forms part of the Public Maritime Domain (DPM), which is inalienable and imprescriptible. Furthermore, underwater remains benefits from heritage status under the Maritime Cultural Property (BCM) designation, that prevents unauthorised removal. Finally, spatial organisation documents such as Territorial Coherence Schemes (SCoT) and Local Urban Plans (PLU(i)) play an important role in enhancing the protection of the serial property and ensuring that the buffer zone effectively provides an added layer of protection. The implementation of a new governance improving the management of the serial property and its buffer zone, while respecting the responsibilities and duties of each managing body, will further enhance the protection of the serial property and its attributes. The governance system for the serial property is structured around the decision-making body (Steering Committee, which will become Property Committee), the consultative body (Territorial Conference), the expert body (Interpretation Committee) and the advisory body (International Scientific Council). The operational implementation of the management of the serial property will be entrusted to the Local Management Committees, with support from an operational task force. Challenges related to the preservation of the serial property are addressed through a number of actions detailed in the management plan. The continuing role of the serial property in education, youth engagement, and multinational commemoration is crucial to ensure that it reflects international collaboration and responsibility.

Name: Ancient Buddhist Site of Sarnath

Short Description: The serial property contains the architectural and archaeological remains of Sarnath, the sacred site where the Buddha is believed to have delivered his first sermon in the 6th century BCE and met his earliest disciples. Identified by the Buddha himself as one of the four principal Buddhist pilgrimage sites, Sarnath grew over many centuries through royal, monastic, and lay patronage, resulting in the construction of numerous stupas, temples, and viharas. After flourishing as a major Buddhist centre, Sarnath declined in the 12th century CE and fell into obscurity until its rediscovery in the 18th century. Today preserved as two archaeological zones, it remains both an important tourist destination and a revived pilgrimage site for Buddhists worldwide.

Description: The serial property contains the architectural and archaeological remains of Sarnath, the sacred site where the Buddha is believed to have delivered his first sermon in the 6th century BCE and met his earliest disciples. Identified by the Buddha himself as one of the four principal Buddhist pilgrimage sites, Sarnath grew over many centuries through royal, monastic, and lay patronage, resulting in the construction of numerous stupas, temples, and viharas. After flourishing as a major Buddhist centre, Sarnath declined in the 12th century CE and fell into obscurity until its rediscovery in the 18th century. Today preserved as two archaeological zones, it remains both an important tourist destination and a revived pilgrimage site for Buddhists worldwide.

Justification: Brief synthesis Located within Varanasi city, state of Uttar Pradesh, India, this serial property composed of two component parts (Chaukhandi Stupa, and the Archaeological Remains of Sarnath) comprises all the known and preserved archaeological and architectural vestiges of the ancient site of Sarnath, believed to be the place that Gautama Buddha visited in the 6th century BCE. Defined by the Buddha as one of the four key sites of Buddhist pilgrimage, Sarnath developed over centuries through royal, monastic and lay patronage. Numerous stupas, temples and viharas were constructed in different historical periods, with evidence from the pre-Mauryan period, through the Kushana and Gupta periods, until the decline of the place in the 12th century CE. Re-discovered in the 18th century, the property is being revived by the Buddhist community as one of their holy places. In the Buddhist tradition, Sarnath is known as Rishipatana, Ishipatana, Mrigadava or the Deer Park, which refer to a sacred geography, where the Buddha is believed to have delivered his first sermon and met his first disciples. Criterion (iii): Ancient Buddhist Site, Sarnath, Varanasi bears witness to the enduring spiritual significance of Sarnath, one of the four principal destinations of Buddhist pilgrimage, established by the Buddha himself, as demonstrated by the large number of religious buildings and other monuments that were built and rebuilt on-site during the many centuries of its existence. While the tradition of pilgrimage is not attested at Sarnath between the 12th century CE and the modern era, the 20th century revival of the practice testifies to the prominent role of this ancient Buddhist site in Buddhist memory and the spiritual imagination. Criterion (vi): Ancient Buddhist Site, Sarnath, Varanasi testifies in a direct and tangible way to the events in the life of the Buddha that are of outstanding significance to the Buddhist community – his first sermon and meeting of his first disciples. The importance of these events and their meaning is carried by the numerous constructions erected at Sarnath over the centuries, which are a response to the message of the Buddha, his teachings, and the concept of Triratna. Integrity The two component parts contain all the known preserved structures of what used to be a Buddhist monastic complex. The common buffer zone reflects their past connection. The serial property has retained its integrity in its essential built elements but its wider original context (the sacred geography), known to be a forested area, has been compromised. The place continues to function as a pilgrimage destination for the Buddhist community. However, the management of the site focuses primarily on its status as an archaeological park, which, in the long term, could affect the spiritual character of the property. Authenticity The archaeological and architectural remains of the monastic complex of Sarnath are authentic in their forms. Conservation efforts undertaken since the early 20th century have ensured preservation of original materials with minimal intervention. The place no longer serves its original function as an active monastic complex but continues to attract Buddhist pilgrims in memory of the first sermon of the Buddha. The recreational use of Sarnath as an archaeological park has an impact on the spirit of the place. The wider setting of the property has been disturbed. Protection and management requirements Both component parts are protected at the highest national level through the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act of 1958 (AMASR Act, amended in 2010). This Act establishes a Prohibited Area covering 100 metres around protected monuments/sites, where any form of construction or development is forbidden, and a Regulated Area extending 200 metres beyond it, in which some construction is allowed subject to approval. Additional protection is provided through planning mechanisms, and particularly the Varanasi Master Plan 2031.The buffer zone is protected through the same measures, with the addition of the regulations pertaining to the Wildlife Protection Act (1972). The Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) is in charge of the protection, conservation, and management of both component parts. The Site Management Plan for the serial property includes recommendations related to conservation.

Cultural Criteria: c3

Name: Alamūt Castle and Related Fortifications

Short Description: The serial property consists of Alamūt Castle and six associated fortifications–Lambesar, Navizaršāh, Šams Kelāyeh, Qosṭinlār, Širkūh, and Ilān–strategically positioned within the rugged landscape of the Alborz Mountains in Qazvin Province, northern Iran. From the late 11th century CE, Alamūt served as the political, military, and intellectual centre of the Nezāri Ismaʿilis, an influential Islamic movement whose reach extended across Iran and the wider Islamic world. This fortified network functioned both as a refuge and as a scholarly and cultural hub, sustaining the Nezāri community until the fall of Alamūt in 1256 and continuing to shape regional religious and intellectual history long thereafter. Together, the fortifications illustrate the strategic organisation, resilience, and cultural significance of the Nezāri Ismaʿili state.

Description: The serial property consists of Alamūt Castle and six associated fortifications–Lambesar, Navizaršāh, Šams Kelāyeh, Qosṭinlār, Širkūh, and Ilān–strategically positioned within the rugged landscape of the Alborz Mountains in Qazvin Province, northern Iran. From the late 11th century CE, Alamūt served as the political, military, and intellectual centre of the Nezāri Ismaʿilis, an influential Islamic movement whose reach extended across Iran and the wider Islamic world. This fortified network functioned both as a refuge and as a scholarly and cultural hub, sustaining the Nezāri community until the fall of Alamūt in 1256 and continuing to shape regional religious and intellectual history long thereafter. Together, the fortifications illustrate the strategic organisation, resilience, and cultural significance of the Nezāri Ismaʿili state.

Justification: Brief synthesis The Alamūt Castle and Related Fortifications are located in the Alborz Mountains of northern Iran, south of the Caspian Sea, within the historic region of Daylamān. The serial property comprises seven castles and fortifications distributed across the Alamūt Valley in Qazvin Province. At its centre stands Alamūt Castle, positioned on a steep rocky outcrop and serving as the headquarters of the Nezāri Ismaʿili state founded by Ḥasan Ṣabbāḥ in 1090. The other component parts – Lambesar Castle, Navizaršāh Castle, Šams Kelāyeh Fortification, Qosṭinlār Fortification, Širkūh Fortification, and Ilān Fortification – are strategically located across the valley and together form a coordinated defensive system. From the late 11th to the mid-13th centuries, Alamūt served as the political, religious, administrative and intellectual centre of the Nezāri Ismaʿili state, which flourished in this mountainous region. The fortifications enabled the organisation, governance, and defence of this community within a naturally protected setting. The Outstanding Universal Value of the serial property is conveyed through the remains of the fortresses and their defensive structures, rock-cut architectural features, water storage and supply systems, archaeological remains associated with the fortified sites, and the surrounding mountainous landscape that structured the defensive network. Criterion (iii): Alamūt Castle and Related Fortifications provide a rare testimony to the Nezāri Ismaʿili cultural tradition, which flourished in the Alborz Mountains from the 11th to the 13th centuries. The property reflects a cohesive socio-political, religious, and intellectual system that integrated defence, administration, scholarship, and community life. The network of castles, water management systems, agricultural terraces, and archaeological remains demonstrate the organisation and ingenuity of the Nezāri Ismaʿilis. The property also reflects the close relationship between the fortifications and local communities, founded upon earlier Ismaʿili missionary activity (daʿwa), which supported the castles with labour, resources, and food. The property represents a historical legacy whose influence continues to shape the identity of the Nezāri Ismaʿili community worldwide. Integrity The serial property maintains integrity through the inclusion of seven strategically selected component parts, which together illustrate the interconnected defensive network and the political, religious, and cultural centrality of the Nezāri Ismaʿili state between the 11th and 13th centuries. The component parts include the key attributes necessary to convey the Outstanding Universal Value of the serial property. While some outer views and valley floors have been affected by modern infrastructure and settlements, the functional relationships, intervisibility, and landscape integration of the castles remain largely intact. Archaeological work and conservation interventions at key sites, particularly at the Alamūt Castle and Lambesar Castle, have stabilised structures, supporting a coherent understanding of the defensive system as a whole. Authenticity The serial property retains authenticity through the original form, design, materials, techniques, location, and setting of the fortifications, as well as the spirit and feeling of the Nezāri Ismaʿili space and cultural tradition. Despite their ruined state, surviving structures, rock-cut architecture, and water management systems reflect the original construction methods and integration with the mountainous environment. Conservation and restoration have used traditional materials and techniques, while the surrounding land use and villages continue to support the sense of place. Protection and management requirements The serial property is safeguarded by a robust national legal framework, including heritage, civil, penal, restoration, and environmental laws, complemented by national protective designations for all component parts and buffer zones. Management is coordinated by the Alamūt Cultural Heritage Base under the supervision of the Iranian Ministry of Cultural Heritage, Tourism and Handicrafts, and is guided by a comprehensive management plan that covers research, conservation, restoration, tourism, and local community engagement. Conservation and monitoring rely on traditional techniques, ongoing archaeological investigation, and a structured multi-level system for the serial property and its buffer zones. Continuing research-based conservation, strengthening preventive monitoring, managing visitor access in accordance with safety and heritage sensitivity, including Heritage Impact Assessment mechanisms into the management system and ensuring long-term staffing and resources, are essential for the long-term preservation of the Outstanding Universal Value of the property.

Cultural Criteria: c3

Name: Mount Amel Castles

Short Description: The serial property comprises five fortified sites located across the historic region of Jabal Amel in southern Lebanon: Qalaat Al Chakif (Beaufort Castle), Qalaat Tibnin (Toron Castle), Qalaat Chakra (Dubieh Castle), Qalaat Deir Kifa (Maron Castle), and Qalaat Chama’ (Chama’ Castle). Occupying prominent hilltops and strategic ridges overlooking major regional routes, the castles formed an integrated defensive and administrative network that controlled movement, communication, and agricultural resources across a vast territory. Developed between the medieval period and the 19th century, they illustrate successive phases of occupation and adaptation by Crusader, Ayyubid, Mamluk, Ottoman, and local feudal rulers. Their fortifications, keeps, towers, gateways, and residential quarters preserve evidence of the continuous exchange of military knowledge, construction techniques, and territorial management practices between European and Near Eastern traditions, while demonstrating the evolution of defensive architecture and fortified network over nearly a millennium.

Name: The Cemetery Complexes of the Xiongnu Nobility

Short Description: This serial property comprises eight funerary complexes of the Xiongnu nobility. The Xiongnu, ancient predecessors of a confederation of Eurasian nomadic peoples, established a powerful empire between the 3rd century BCE and the 2nd century CE that eventually occupied a vast territory centred on what is now Mongolia. They interacted with the Han Chinese and controlled nodes along the main parts of the Steppe Route of the Silk Roads. Among the numerous archaeological remains found across the former expanse of the empire, their cemeteries provide important insights into Xiongnu burial culture. The main burials, notable for their substantial size and depth, are accompanied by satellite graves marked by small ring-shaped mounds, as well as sacrificial structures consisting of alignments of paired stones. A wide range of artefacts found in the tombs, including horse tack and chariots as well as weapons, tools and food for the afterlife, provides a window into the Xiongnu way of life and social structure. The tombs of the Xiongnu nobility highlight the engineering and organisational skills of this predominantly nomadic culture.

Justification: Brief synthesis This serial property comprises eight funerary complexes of the Xiongnu nobility. The Xiongnu, ancient predecessors of a confederation of Eurasian nomadic peoples, established a powerful empire between the 3rd century BCE and the 2nd century CE that occupied a vast territory centred on what is now the modern state of Mongolia. They interacted with the Han Chinese and controlled nodes along the main parts of the Steppe Route of the Silk Roads. Among the numerous archaeological traces throughout the area occupied by the empire are their cemeteries, which provide insights into their burial culture. Of substantial size and depth, the main burials are accompanied by satellite graves (with small ring-shaped mounds) as well as sacrificial structures (lines of stone pairs). A wide range of artefacts found in the tombs, including horse tack and chariots as well as weapons, tools and food for the afterlife, provides a window into the Xiongnu way of life and social structure. The tombs of their nobility highlight the engineering and organisational skills of this mainly nomadic culture. Criterion (iii): The Cemetery Complexes of the Xiongnu Nobility testify in an exceptional way to the extinct Xiongnu funerary culture. They provide insights into the burial customs, rituals, established traditions and tomb construction of the nomadic Xiongnu nobles. Even though there exists already more than a century of research on these tombs, much about the Xiongnu funerary culture, with its burial customs and rituals, is still unknown or not well understood. These tombs with their deep burial chambers, satellite graves and sacrificial structures, as well as with their rich offerings, make the serial property an exceptional testimony to the extinct Xiongnu funerary culture. The serial property is an exceptional expression of, and the richest source of insight into, the functioning of this culture of the Central Asian Steppe. Integrity Each one of the eight component parts contributes to the series in a substantial way. Together, they represent the regional characteristics of Xiongnu tombs across the administrative and territorial divisions of the Xiongnu empire. They also cover the chronological span of the Xiongnu empire, and include examples of different expressions of the Xiongnu funerary culture, thus constituting a representational sample of Xiongnu cemetery complexes. The conditions of integrity of the individual tombs are adequate, though it has been affected by acts of looting that caused some destruction. Of the thirty-nine excavated tombs, thirty-eight were disturbed. However, even the disturbed tombs provide important insights into the Xiongnu funerary culture and offer valuable artefacts that throw light on the social dimension of Xiongnu society and their beliefs. It is of note that the state of underground vestiges that have never been excavated is to a large extent unconfirmed. Apart from the looting, other factors potentially affecting the property are adequately controlled. The boundaries of each component part are sufficiently large in order to contain all the known attributes and convey the Outstanding Universal Value of the property. The study of the relationship of the funerary complexes with their wider setting will enhance the integrity of the property. Authenticity The component parts preserve the original forms and layouts of the different funerary structures, as well as their original locations. The remoteness of most of the component parts as well as the slow soil formation processes in Mongolia have helped to minimise changes to their settings. The archaeological contexts have suffered the usual changes due to decomposition of organic materials and movements of the soil. Old methods of post-excavation backfilling might have also led to some disturbances. Protection and management requirements The serial property is legally protected at both national and provincial levels. All of the component parts are under the jurisdiction of the State Party. Except for the Cemetery Complex of the Xiongnu Nobility at Chikhertiin Zoo (component part 1), all the sites are included in the List of Immovable Historical and Cultural Heritage Properties under State, Provincial and Local Protection (2020). Local authorities are legally responsible for the protection of the sites. Relevant national laws protecting cultural heritage include the Law on Protection of Cultural Heritage of Mongolia (2015), the Law on Special Protected Areas of Mongolia (1994), and the Law on Buffer Zones of Protected Areas (1997). A World Heritage Protection Administration, modelled after the Noyon Uul Special Protection Administration that was established for the Noyon Uul Protected Area in 2024, will be created. This management structure will implement the management plan for The Cemetery Complexes of the Xiongnu Nobility in cooperation with the Special Protection Administration of the Noyon Uul Protected Area, and the Mongolian National Committee for World Heritage will provide the World Heritage Protection Administration with professional guidance and recommendations.

Cultural Criteria: c3

Name: Gdynia Modernist City Centre

Short Description: Located on the Baltic Sea coast, Gdynia Modernist City Centre encompasses the two most significant east-west and north-south streets, featuring interwar planning blocks and the majority of the city centre’s preserved buildings from that period, which reflect the large-scale application of modernist ideas in architectural design. The result is an urban organism that harnesses a building-block-based planning approach to develop a characteristic, compact complex of modernist architecture, with robust individual architectural expressions. The city centre, with its buildings, villas on Kamienna Góra hill, and other residential buildings of this period, illustrates a critical break with historicism in the progression of turning the village of Gdynia into a new major sea gateway of the first Polish Republic between the First and Second World Wars.

Name: Sebastia

Justification: Brief synthesis Located northwest of Nablus, in the West Bank, Sebastia is a multi-period mound site that preserves archaeological and architectural vestiges that testify to its occupation by different civilisations, with different intensity, from the 9th century BCE. The layered structure of the property includes remains that testify to the inhabitation of the site in the Iron Age, when it was a prominent regional political centre, widely identified with the ancient city of Samaria; to the Hellenistic period, when it became a fortified stronghold; to the Roman period when the city was renamed Sebaste by Herod and acquired the status of a Roman colony under Septimius Severus; to the Byzantine period when the importance of the city declined but it became a seat of a bishopric; and finally to later historical phases dating to the medieval period (especially the Crusader era) and the Ottoman era. The successive cultural layers allow to trace the political, religious and urban history of Samaria/Sebaste, while still offering an exceptional potential for future scientific research. Criterion (iii): The visible coexistence, within a single archaeological site, and the exceptional legibility of material traces left by the successive civilisations that occupied this place from the Iron Age, through the Hellenistic and Roman periods, to the Byzantine period, as well as later additions from the Crusader era, makes Sebastia stand out within the Levant region. With its multi-layered character and multi-period evidence, the property represents a coherent ensemble that testifies to the principal historical phases of the settlement of the site. Unlike many continuously inhabited cities where successive urban development has obscured earlier remains, Sebastia preserves relatively direct archaeological traces of its major periods of development which allows for a clear reading of successive political, religious, and urban systems that remain physically interconnected. Integrity The multi-layered site of Sebastia includes all the known archaeological remains and architectural structures that testify to the occupation of the site from the Iron Age until the Byzantine period, as well as several notable Crusader period vestiges. The physical conditions of the property could not have been fully evaluated the time of inscription due to the lack of a technical evaluation mission, but the state of its physical fabric seems to be uneven, with some sections of the property in a worse state than others due to the combined effects of weathering, erosion, vegetation growth, and prolonged exposure of excavated remains. The integrity of the site is currently threatened by the land expropriation plans, aimed at dividing the property and developing the Shomron National Park in its western section. Considering further the existing threats related to the ongoing Israeli-Palestinian conflict and the developmental pressures, the integrity of the property can be considered as highly vulnerable. Authenticity The different historical layers within the property remain legible and continue to communicate the heritage values that underpin the significance of the site through the preserved vestiges, even if the earliest archaeological evidence has been partially damaged by subsequent historical developments, since the successive civilisations built their cities amidst or on top of the previous ones. In the absence of a technical evaluation mission, the full assessment of the authenticity of the property was not possible at the time of inscription. Protection and management requirements The property is protected by the Decree Law of Tangible Cultural Heritage (No. 11, 2018), and its protection, management and conservation are overseen by the Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities. The Sebastia Municipality oversees implementation of planning controls and coordinates with the Ministry in the regulation of development activities. The site is included as a protected area within the 2018 Municipal Spatial Master Plan and is managed through the 2020 Conservation and Management Plan; both of these documents will be revised to ensure the effective protection of the property in accordance with the approved boundaries. While adequate legal frameworks, additional planning instruments and conservation strategies formally exist, the practical application of the governance system is constrained by the existing territorial division of the site into Area B (administered under Palestinian civil control and joint Israeli-Palestinian security control) and Area C (under full Israeli control) resulting from the Oslo Accords, which was intended to be a temporary measure.

Cultural Criteria: c3

Name: Wat Phra Mahathat Woramahawihan, Nakhon Si Thammarat

Short Description: Wat Phra Mahathat Woramahawihan (or Phra Mahathat monastery), located in Nakhon Si Thammarat Province in Peninsular Thailand on a narrow ridge between the Pacific and Indian oceans, has served as a major regional Buddhist centre since its founding in the 8th century. Benefiting from the transoceanic trade networks, the monastery was influenced by various religious and architectural traditions including Brahmanism, Hinduism, Mahayana Buddhism and Theravada Buddhism from northeastern India, central Java, Sri Lanka and the Mon region of southern Myanmar. These influences have been integrated into its religious buildings, rituals and cultural traditions. Its distinctive artistic and architectural expressions have exerted a wide-ranging and enduring influence throughout Thailand and across Southeast Asia. The religious and local traditions have continued at the monastery for more than 1,500 years, including the Nakhon Si Thammarat chronicle tradition, the annual cloth-wrapping ceremony for the Great Reliquary and the Nora dance drama.

Justification: Brief synthesis Wat Phra Mahathat Woramahawihan (or Phra Mahathat monastery) is a Theravada Buddhist monastery located in the Nakhon Si Thammarat Province in Peninsular Thailand, a crucial trade crossroad between the Indian and Pacific Oceans. Founded in the 8th century, where a Hindu shrine once stood (5th-8th centuries), the monastery has been a regional religious centre ever since. The complex is centred on the Great Reliquary of Buddha in the form of a mandala (Buddhavasa), flanked by the residential quarters of the monks (Sanghavasa) to the north and south according to the Tipiṭaka (Pali Canon). It comprises religious buildings, including the Great Reliquary with satellite stupas, various functional structures, two Bodhi tree shrines and the sacred Crystal Beach, on which the monastery is built, as well as residential buildings in the monastery. Bearing witness to the fusion of Brahmanism, Hinduism and the Mahayana and Theravada Buddhism of South and Southeast Asia, the combined artistic and architectural expressions found at Wat Phra Mahathat, imbued with local and religious traditions, had a lasting influence on building construction in the region. Criterion (ii): Wat Phra Mahathat is an exceptional testament to the interchange of human values. The Great Reliquary demonstrates the influence of Brahmanism, Hinduism and the Mahayana and Theravada schools of Buddhism, originating from Pala art in Nalanda, Central Javanese art, Sri Lankan art and Mon art from southern Myanmar. In turn, the combined architectural style of the Great Reliquary has exerted a profound influence on subsequent religious buildings in Thailand, Malaysia and beyond. Criterion (vi): As the testimony to diverse belief systems and the spiritual centre of Nakhon Si Thammarat, Wat Phra Mahathat is the heart of living religious traditions with artistic and literary works of outstanding universal significance, such as the Nora dance drama and the local chronicles. These traditions vividly represent the relationships between this sacred site and its surrounding communities and inspired other monasteries and communities in Thailand and beyond. Integrity The boundaries of the property follow the outline of Wat Phra Mahathat, which is large enough to include all the attributes conveying the Outstanding Universal Value. The mandala plan of the Great Reliquary complex, the Tipikata layout of the monastery, all the religious buildings and the Crystal Beach on which the monastery was established, are all included in the property. Important views and settings are protected by the buffer zone. The property is in a good state of conservation, and well-maintained by the monastery and local communities, as well as relevant authorities. The modern urban development has no negative impact on the area inside the monastery, and all factors affecting the property are under control. Authenticity The property retains a high level of authenticity in terms of location, function, form, materials, traditions, and spirit. The location and function of the monastery remain unchanged since its establishment in the 8th century. The layouts of the Great Reliquary and the monastery have been authentically preserved. The forms and traces of architectural and artistic expressions of different origins since the 8th century have been preserved at the Great Reliquary stupa. Traditional materials and techniques have been used in the past restorations, which preserved the original forms of religious buildings. The living Bodhi trees testify to the authentic roots of their origin. The sacred sand ground is still preserved. The Phra Mahathat Monastery is still active, continuing its associated traditions. Protection and management requirements The property is inscribed on the List of National Ancient Monuments and has been registered in the Royal Gazette in 1936 and 2024. It is protected under the Act on Ancient Monuments, Antiques, Objects of Art and National Museums (currently under revision) and the Sangha Act, which both provide the highest level of protection at the national level. The buffer zone covers the important views and settings and is protected by a comprehensive framework of legislations and planning regulations at the provincial and municipality levels. Within the buffer zone, a height control zone has been demarcated for protecting the important views. The management framework comprises institutions from national, provincial and municipal levels, and is featured by a combination of traditional and State management, with active participation of local communities. The management activities are guided by the Management Plan of Wat Phra Mahathat (2026-2030) and are supported by the Disaster and Human-Induced Risk Management Plan for the Cultural World Heritage Site, Wat Phra Mahathat Woramahawihan, Nakhon Si Thammarat Province, Thailand, as well as Tourism Management Plan for the Conservation of Cultural Heritage: Wat Phra Mahathat Woramahawihan (2026-2030) developed specially for the monastery.

Cultural Criteria: c2

Name: Tashkent Modernist Architecture. Modernity and Tradition in Central Asia

Short Description: The property embodies a representative ensemble of ten modernist buildings and urban complexes constructed between the 1960s and early 1990s, a formative period in the reconstruction and transformation of Tashkent following the 1966 earthquake. The series includes museums, exhibition halls, residential ensembles, cultural institutions, and scientific or infrastructural facilities, reflecting the broad functional spectrum of late‑Soviet architectural production. Nine out of ten component parts are situated along the newly planned urban axes of the reconstructed city centre, as defined in successive masterplans that reshaped Tashkent into a modern socialist metropolis. Together, they articulate the city’s principal public spaces and demonstrate the integration of modernist planning principles with local climatic, seismic, and cultural conditions. Collectively, the serial property illustrates a distinct phase of architectural modernism characterised by industrialised construction, seismic‑resilient engineering, and the adaptation of standardised systems to regional materials, traditions, and environmental constraints.

text:
Name: Jingdezhen Handicraft Porcelain Industry Sites

Short Description: The serial property portrays the evolution of the production of handicraft porcelain from the 10th to 19th centuries that had profound industrial, artistic and trading influences in China and beyond globally. The five component parts reflect the processes of the production of porcelain, including the extraction and transportation of raw materials, innovations in kiln design and the spatial and social organisation of production on an immense scale. The town area featured the Imperial Kiln alongside civilian kilns, guilds and merchant associations. Jingdezhen was a centre of technological innovation in porcelain production, including the “binary formula” of mixing kaolin and porcelain stone. Porcelain of the highest quality was produced at Jingdezhen, and its blue-and-white porcelain and designs became a prized global commodity and a symbol of Chinese culture and artistry.

Description: The serial property portrays the evolution of the production of handicraft porcelain from the 10th to 19th centuries that had profound industrial, artistic and trading influences in China and beyond globally. The five component parts reflect the processes of the production of porcelain, including the extraction and transportation of raw materials, innovations in kiln design and the spatial and social organisation of production on an immense scale. The town area featured the Imperial Kiln alongside civilian kilns, guilds and merchant associations. Jingdezhen was a centre of technological innovation in porcelain production, including the “binary formula” of mixing kaolin and porcelain stone. Porcelain of the highest quality was produced at Jingdezhen, and its blue-and-white porcelain and designs became a prized global commodity and a symbol of Chinese culture and artistry.

Justification: Brief synthesis The Jingdezhen Handicraft Porcelain Industry Sites are located in an area with rich reserves of porcelain stone, kaolin clay, firewood forests and water transportation. Five component parts represent the handicraft porcelain industry system of Jingdezhen from the 10th to the 19th century. Together they exhibit the innovative development of Chinese porcelain making technology and porcelain art that had a profound impact on the development of the ceramic industry of the world. From the 10th to the 13th centuries integration of the porcelain-making technologies of northern and southern China achieved the stable production of bluish-white porcelain and laid the foundation for Jingdezhen to develop into a Chinese porcelain production centre. In the 13th-15th centuries, innovations included the “binary formula” (mixing porcelain stone with kaolin), new kiln forms, and the use of imported cobalt pigments to produce the blue-and-white porcelain. From the 16th century, Jingdezhen was the handicraft porcelain production centre of the world, supported by a complex industrial structure that connected porcelain manufacturing and sales centres with raw material and firewood production areas via a waterway transportation system. The Jingdezhen Handicraft Porcelain Industry Sites bear witness to the formation of a large-scale intensive production model characterised by an industrial chain with fine divisions of labour, standardisation and specialisation, leading to a capacity for high quality porcelain. Through the advancement of production technologies and industrial organisation, Jingdezhen maintained its position as the porcelain production centre of the world from the 16th century, promoting the widespread dissemination of Chinese porcelain making technology, art and products around the world. Criterion (ii): The Jingdezhen Handicraft Porcelain Industry Sites demonstrate global exchanges in porcelain-making technologies and art, and innovations in porcelain production from the 10th to the 19th centuries. The Hutian Ancient Kiln Site portrays the integration of porcelain-making technologies for bluish-white porcelain from the north and south of China from the 10th-13th centuries. The development of technologies at Jingdezhen during the 13th-19th centuries combined traditional Chinese porcelain-making with Middle Eastern, Chinese and European pigments, and a fusion of Chinese and foreign decorative techniques to produce blue-and-white, enamel and famille-rose porcelain. The “binary formula” technology attracted widespread attention and was an important inspiration and influence on the development of high-temperature hard-paste porcelain technology in Europe during the 18th century. Jingdezhen became a world porcelain production centre from the 16th-18th centuries, with its artistic styles studied and imitated all over the world. Criterion (iii): The Jingdezhen Handicraft Porcelain Industry Sites exhibit the continuous production process of the porcelain industry from the 10th to the 19th centuries and a complete industrial pattern including the social organisation of production. The five component parts provide a testimony to the tradition of Chinese handicraft porcelain industry. Criterion (iv): The Jingdezhen Handicraft Porcelain Industry Sites are a technological ensemble that illustrates important stages in the development of the handicraft porcelain industry, an outstanding example of innovation in global porcelain technologies, art and industrial organisation from the 13th to the 19th centuries. The uses of raw materials at Jingdezhen, the “binary formula” technology, modelling technologies, kiln designs, and innovations in underglaze and overglaze decoration techniques enriched the diversity of porcelain shapes and decorative styles. The large-scale industrial spatial layout, division of labour, and specialised and standardised production model enabled the efficient and high-quality porcelain production at Jingdezhen. Criterion (vi): As an important vehicle of Chinese culture and an important symbol of Oriental art, evidence of blue-and-white porcelain of Jingdezhen establishes a direct association with European decorative art from the 17th-18th centuries. As a global high-end trade commodity, the blue-and-white porcelain of Jingdezhen is one of the core elements of “chinoiserie” that was popular in Europe. These artistic elements were widely collected and used in pattern design, painting, furniture, architectural decoration and other fields, with porcelain serving as a medium to promote the global expression of Chinese culture. Integrity The five component parts include raw material sources, kilns, workshops, transportation and other production facilities that demonstrate the elements and stages of the development of the handicraft porcelain technology of Jingdezhen from the 10th to the 19th century. They include buildings used for the social organisation and management, commercial and trade activities, religious and belief practices, and the porcelain production tools and products of Jingdezhen. The Jingdezhen Handicraft Porcelain Industry Sites include a full suite of relevant attributes of the industrial system of porcelain production including the spatial layouts, production facilities and technological processes, and social organisation. The boundaries are appropriately delineated and ensure the protection of the key attributes. The component parts are generally in a good state of conservation, and potential threats are well identified. Authenticity The attributes include archaeological sites, historic buildings, wharves, mining sites, firewood forests, historic roads, and sections of rivers, as well as intangible cultural heritage practices associated with porcelain production. The scale of the porcelain production centre is verified by a series of kiln sites along the east bank of the Changjiang River and the depth of kiln accumulations in the town area. The spatial layout of the porcelain production centre, raw material and firewood production areas, urban and rural environmental settings, and the historic river sections connecting the component parts demonstrate the organisation of the handicraft porcelain industry of Jingdezhen. The authenticity of the attributes has been established by historical maps and literature, and by past and continuing archaeological and historical research. Porcelain making is still the pillar industry in Jingdezhen with continuing community involvement. Protection and management requirements The protection of the Jingdezhen Handicraft Porcelain Industry Sites is supported by national and provincial laws and regulations, including the Law of the People’s Republic of China on the Protection of Cultural Relics (and its regulations), the Regulations of Jiangxi Province for the Conservation of Cultural Heritage, and the Regulations of Jingdezhen Municipality for the Conservation of Handicraft Porcelain Industry Heritage. The five component parts and their buffer zones are incorporated into the territory spatial planning framework. Intangible cultural heritage elements are safeguarded by the Intangible Cultural Heritage Law of the People’s Republic of China and the Regulations of Jiangxi Province on the Intangible Cultural Heritage. A four-level management framework has been established, consisting of the State, Jiangxi Province, Jingdezhen City, and the Jingdezhen Handicraft Porcelain Industry Heritage Conservation Center. This Center is responsible for the coordinated management of the property. The component parts are managed by the Zhushan District and Changjiang District Cultural Heritage Bureaus, the Jingdezhen Imperial Kiln Institute, the Jingdezhen Ceramic Culture Inheritance and Innovation Center, the Gaoling-Yaoli Scenic and Historic Area Management Committee and Fuliang County Cultural Heritage Bureau. The Conservation Management Plan of the Serial Property of “Jingdezhen Handicraft Porcelain Industry Sites” (2025-2035) identifies objectives and specific activities for the conservation, protection and interpretation of the property, including monitoring and stakeholder coordination, community participation in decision-making processes and capacity building. Heritage Impact Assessment processes are in place for each of the component parts. A research plan is in place, and a number of strategies and measures are implemented to manage congestion at heavily visited sites.

Cultural Criteria: c2, c3, c4

Name: The system of Italian-style condominio theatres of the 18th and 19th centuries in Central Italy

Short Description: The serial property comprises ten Italian‑style condominio theatres built between the mid‑18th and late 19th centuries across Emilia‑Romagna, Marche, and Umbria in central Italy. Architecturally representative of Neoclassicism with Late Baroque influences, these theatres feature tiered boxes, carefully designed auditoriums for optimal acoustics and visibility, stalls, foyers, ridotti, and historic stage machinery. They embody the innovative “condominio” system, a model of collective ownership and public‑private financing that enabled municipalities and private citizens to collaborate in constructing theatres in small and medium‑sized towns. This system fostered the growth of a widespread cultural network, providing new representational spaces for the emerging bourgeoisie and broadening public access to the performing arts. Located at the heart of historic town centres, these theatres became important civic meeting places, hosting performances and public events and contributing to the formation of public opinion.

Description: The serial property comprises ten Italian‑style condominio theatres built between the mid‑18th and late 19th centuries across Emilia‑Romagna, Marche, and Umbria in central Italy. Architecturally representative of Neoclassicism with Late Baroque influences, these theatres feature tiered boxes, carefully designed auditoriums for optimal acoustics and visibility, stalls, foyers, ridotti, and historic stage machinery. They embody the innovative “condominio” system, a model of collective ownership and public‑private financing that enabled municipalities and private citizens to collaborate in constructing theatres in small and medium‑sized towns. This system fostered the growth of a widespread cultural network, providing new representational spaces for the emerging bourgeoisie and broadening public access to the performing arts. Justification: Brief synthesis The condominio theatre represents a major evolution in the Italian-style theatre model around the mid-18th and late 19th centuries, marking the transition from being a place for aristocratic entertainment to becoming a cultural institution driven by an emerging bourgeoisie. Based on a unique partnership between public bodies and groups of wealthy citizens, known as società condominiali, this economic model is founded on collective ownership and the sharing of costs. This management structure enabled the wide spread of theatres, particularly in small and medium-sized towns in Italy. By making the financers of theatre projects partners in their design, the condominio model turned these theatres into spaces for architectural experimentation and as economic driving forces for these small and medium-sized towns. The condominio model thus fostered the development of specific architectural features manifesting themselves in precise adjustments to social spaces (entrance halls, foyer, ridotto), the standardisation of the tiered boxes, the optimisation of sightlines, the development of separate circulation systems, transforming the theatre into a tool of prestige precisely tailored for its users. This model fostered the emergence of spaces for social life where culture belonged to an emerging bourgeoisie. In addition to their artistic purpose, these theatres have also played a role as centres of political awareness, transforming small and medium-sized towns into dynamic social and cultural centres; a function they still retain today. Criterion (iii): The system of Italian-style condominio theatres of the 18th and 19th centuries in Central Italy bears witness to the rapid development in town centres of a phenomenon that saw widespread expansion in the 19th century in Italy and Europe, followed by Latin America. These theatres, which first appeared in the provinces of Emilia-Romagna, Marche and Umbria from around the mid-18th century on, were one of the few places where groups of representatives of the emerging bourgeoisie, patrons of the theatres, could gather, and where public opinion was formed. These theatres, financed via the società condominiali involving public bodies and private citizens in the construction and management of these spaces, embody the transition from an exclusive private domain to civic institutions accessible to a wide audience. The condominio theatres of the regions of Emilia-Romagna, Marche and Umbria, part of the former Papal States, enabled the development of innovative solutions for theatres, reflecting the participation of different social classes and testifying to the new social hierarchy. The longevity of these theatres, which continue to host a wide variety of cultural events today, bears witness to how deeply they are embedded in local community life. Integrity The ten component parts comprising the serial property include the most emblematic examples of condominio theatres. The component parts share all of the defining features developed during the three historical periods under consideration, from the early 18th to the late 19th centuries. Each of the component parts continues to serve the purpose for which it was originally created. The component parts are in a good general state of conservation and, when conservation works are needed, these are scheduled. Authenticity The serial property meets the conditions of authenticity in terms of form and design, materials, use and function, location and setting. All component parts convey the Outstanding Universal Value of the property through a series of common attributes: the financing model through the società condominiali; the continuity of use; and the physical and spatial features of the Italian-style theatre as codified by condominio theatres. Numerous written and visual sources are able to confirm the authenticity of the theatres of the serial property, providing key information for understanding their history and development. Archival documents, including original plans and those of subsequent restorations demonstrate the care taken with the structures and their decorative elements. Protection and management requirements Responsibility for the protection and management of each of the ten component parts of the serial property lies with the national government, and local, regional and municipal authorities. Each component part is protected by town planning regulations and legislation applicable nationally or locally, as well as by public ownership. The main legislative framework is governed by the Cultural Heritage and Landscape Code; Legislative Decree 42/2004 of 22 January 2004, and law 1089/1939 of 1 June 1939. The management system of the serial property is based on the Memorandum of Understanding established between the Ministry of Culture (MiC) and the three regions and municipalities concerned. This agreement defines the roles and responsibilities of these authorities for the long-term conservation and management of the property.

Cultural Criteria: c3
