Name: Aqaba Marine Reserve

Short Description: The property, located at the northernmost tip of the Red Sea, comprises a mosaic of coral reefs, seagrass beds, and mesophotic reefs that sustain diverse marine life and ecological processes. Recognized as the world’s northernmost tropical coral reef system, the property is notable for its thermally resilient corals, which have adapted over the last 10,000 years to marine heatwaves, high salinity, and elevated summer temperatures. The reserve safeguards important marine genetic resources and supports exceptional biodiversity, including more than 150 species of hard coral, over 500 species of fish, and 1,000 species of molluscs. Its coral endemism is globally significant, supporting approximately 61% of all Red Sea endemic hard coral species, while more than 80 fish species are endemic to the Red Sea or Gulf of Aqaba.

Description: The property, located at the northernmost tip of the Red Sea, comprises a mosaic of coral reefs, seagrass beds, and mesophotic reefs that sustain diverse marine life and ecological processes. Recognized as the world’s northernmost tropical coral reef system, the property is notable for its thermally resilient corals, which have adapted over the last 10,000 years to marine heatwaves, high salinity, and elevated summer temperatures. The reserve safeguards important marine genetic resources and supports exceptional biodiversity, including more than 150 species of hard coral, over 500 species of fish, and 1,000 species of molluscs. Its coral endemism is globally significant, supporting approximately 61% of all Red Sea endemic hard coral species, while more than 80 fish species are endemic to the Red Sea or Gulf of Aqaba.

Justification: Brief synthesis The Aqaba Marine Reserve (AMR), located at the northernmost tip of the Red Sea, contains a mosaic of habitats, including coral reefs, seagrass beds, and mesophotic reefs, which collectively sustain diverse marine life and vital ecological processes. These interconnected ecosystems make the AMR a cornerstone for marine biodiversity conservation and protection of threatened marine ecosystems. AMR is globally recognised as the northernmost tropical coral reef system, known for its thermally resilient corals. It is predicted that these corals will remain among the most resilient by the end of century. Moreover, the property hosts numerous endemic species, safeguards unique marine genetic resources, and provides a critical habitat for rare and threatened marine species. Criterion (ix): Eco-evolutionary processes over the last 10,000 years have facilitated the adaptation of coral populations and associated benthic assemblages to hostile climate conditions including marine heatwaves, high salinity, and recurring elevated summer extreme temperatures with limited bleaching and rapid recovery, to the degree possible, in the long term. The thermally resilient corals and other benthic invertebrates in the Gulf of Aqaba have high survival and recovery rates to acute and chronic thermal stress, making the area a critical research site and important genetic repository for understanding climate change-related resilience and restoration. The maintenance of trophic interactions and functional ecology representative of the northern Red Sea’s extreme conditions contributes to the evolutionary processes maintained in situ. Habitats such as seagrass meadows stabilise sediments, sequester carbon, and serve as nurseries for juvenile species. Criterion (x): The benthic and mesophotic ecosystems of the AMR are home to over 150 species of hard coral (of which 40 are assessed as globally threatened at the time of inscription), in addition to over 500 species of fish and 1000 species of molluscs. The property’s coral endemism is globally significant, supporting approximately 61% of all Red Sea endemic hard coral species. Over 80% of all fish species in AMR are associated with benthic habitats with over 80 species endemic to the Red Sea or Gulf of Aqaba. Integrity The AMR effectively encompasses all major habitats, including shallow and mesophotic coral reefs and seagrass beds, necessary for ecological functionality. While compact, it is of a sufficient size, to enable key processes including, intra reef reproduction and larval recruitment of heat adapted species for the ongoing in situ adaptation to thermal stress and nutrient cycling. A buffer zone surrounds the entire property and supports the ecological resilience of these species’ communities. The state of conservation of AMR’s marine natural features, at the time of inscription, is secure and well preserved with intact ecological communities and functioning biological processes that maintain ecological integrity. Although being effectively mitigated, the property is particularly prone to impacts from external pollution, water quality and tourism-related impacts due to its close proximity to significant infrastructure. A robust and continued monitoring system to monitor and respond to these threats is essential to maintaining the long-term integrity and high ecosystem health of the property and minimise impacts. Protection and management requirements The AMR is designated nationally as a protected area and benefits from a multi-layered governance and management regime led by the Aqaba Special Economic Zone Authority (ASEZA) under the Aqaba Marine Reserve Bylaw and its associated regulations. The management of the reserve is overseen by the AMR Management Committee, consisting of a wide variety of relevant local, national and international stakeholders. The day-to-day management of the property is guided by the AMR Management Plan focusing on ecosystem preservation, biodiversity monitoring, and sustainable tourism in furtherance of AMR’s primary conservation objectives. Regulations on fishing, tourism, and other activities, along with the enforcement of restricted and prohibited zones, ensure the conservation and long-term sustainability of the reserve’s coral reef ecosystems and associated biodiversity. The protection framework also prioritises scientific research, education, and stakeholder and local community engagement, with collaborative efforts involving international research institutions to advance coral resilience and global conservation strategies. Given the property’s small size and location, effective protection and management of the property also relies on the sustained strong collaboration with and support of other Jordanian national institutions, including the Maritime Commission, Environmental Police, Navy and Coast Guard, the Aqaba Container Terminal and other shipping operations, tourism operators and local communities.

Natural Criteria: n9, n10

Name: Boma–Badingilo Migratory Landscape

Short Description: The property comprises Boma National Park, Badingilo National Park, and the surrounding floodplain and savanna landscapes in South Sudan. Located at the interface between the Sudd wetland system and the East Sudanian Savanna, it encompasses an extensive mosaic of seasonally flooded grasslands, wetlands, floodplains, woodlands, and savannas shaped by seasonal rainfall and flood dynamics. These interconnected ecosystems sustain one of the world’s largest remaining terrestrial mammal migrations, with an estimated six million White-eared Kob, Tiang, and Mongalla Gazelle moving across a vast and largely unimpeded landscape in response to changing environmental conditions. The site also reflects important cultural, and linguistic diversity of the region with the Murle, Dinka, Nuer, Anyuak and Toposa and other ethnic groups who have been custodians of this landscape through herding, farming and fishing for centuries and even millennia. The property also supports important populations of numerous large mammal species, including Nile Lechwe, African Savanna Elephant, African Wild Dog, Lion, Leopard, Northeastern Africa Cheetah, and Beisa Oryx, as well as significant assemblages of waterbirds, raptors, and migratory bird species. Its exceptional scale, ecological connectivity, habitat diversity, and relative intactness sustain ecological and biological processes that have become increasingly rare globally.

Description: The property comprises Boma National Park, Badingilo National Park, and the surrounding floodplain and savanna landscapes in South Sudan. Located at the interface between the Sudd wetland system and the East Sudanian Savanna, it encompasses an extensive mosaic of seasonally flooded grasslands, wetlands, floodplains, woodlands, and savannas shaped by seasonal rainfall and flood dynamics. The site also reflects important cultural, and linguistic diversity of the region with the Murle, Dinka, Nuer, Anyuak and Toposa and other ethnic groups who have been custodians of this landscape through herding, farming and fishing for centuries and even millennia. The property also supports important populations of numerous large mammal species, including Nile Lechwe, African Savanna Elephant, African Wild Dog, Lion, Leopard, Northeastern Africa Cheetah, and Beisa Oryx, as well as significant assemblages of waterbirds, raptors, and migratory bird species. Its exceptional scale, ecological connectivity, habitat diversity, and relative intactness sustain ecological and biological processes that have become increasingly rare globally.

Justification: Brief synthesis The Boma–Badingilo Migratory Landscape (BBML), covering approximately 11,250,000 hectares in South Sudan, encompasses Boma National Park, Badingilo National Park and the wider floodplain and savanna landscapes that together sustain one of, if not, the world's largest remaining terrestrial mammal migrations. Located at the interface between the Sudd wetland system and the East Sudanian Savanna, the property comprises an extensive mosaic of seasonally flooded grasslands, wetlands, floodplains, woodlands and savannas that support large-scale ecological processes driven by seasonal rainfall and flood dynamics. The property supports the movement of millions of migratory ungulates across a vast and largely unfenced, unimpeded landscape. The migration remains ecologically functional and continues to operate across extensive seasonal habitats and migration corridors, making it one of the last remaining examples of a large-scale terrestrial migration system functioning at a landscape scale. In addition to its migratory wildlife, the property supports important populations of numerous large mammal species, together with significant populations of waterbirds and raptors associated with the floodplain ecosystem. The property's exceptional scale, ecological connectivity and relative intactness underpin ecological and biological processes that have become increasingly rare globally. Criterion (vii): The Boma–Badingilo Migratory Landscape contains one of, if not, the world's most spectacular remaining wildlife migrations. Each year, an estimate six million White-Eared Kob, Tiang and Mongalla Gazelle move across vast floodplains, wetlands and savannas in response to seasonal flooding and changing resource availability. The scale of the migration, extraordinary numbers of animals involved and the largely intact landscape through which it occurs combine to create an exceptional natural phenomenon of global significance, representing one of the last remaining wildlife spectacles of its kind. Criterion (ix): The Boma–Badingilo Migratory Landscape is an outstanding example of ongoing ecological and biological processes associated with large-scale ungulate migration in a seasonally dynamic savanna ecosystem. The interaction between seasonal flooding, corresponding vegetation productivity and associated wildlife movements sustains what is likely to be the largest remaining terrestrial migration of land mammals in the world. The migration system facilitates ecological connectivity across extensive floodplains, wetlands and grasslands and supports ecological processes that have become increasingly rare as comparable migration systems elsewhere have been fragmented or lost. Criterion (x): The property contains significant habitats for the in-situ conservation of biological diversity, including globally important populations of migratory ungulates and numerous threatened species. The BBML supports globally significant populations of White-Eared Kob, Tiang and Mongalla Gazelle together with important populations of Nile Lechwe, African Savanna Elephant, African Wild Dog, Lion, Leopard, Northeastern Africa Cheetah, Beisa Oryx and other species of conservation importance. The extensive and relatively intact floodplain and savanna ecosystems also provide habitat for important assemblages of waterbirds, raptors and migratory bird species associated with the Upper Nile Basin and migratory flyways. The size, ecological connectivity and habitat diversity of the property contribute significantly to its importance for biodiversity conservation within the East Sudanian Savanna and the greater Nile Basin region. Integrity The property includes the principal migration routes, seasonal habitats, floodplains, wetlands and ecological processes necessary to sustain the large-scale migration system for which it is inscribed. Its exceptional scale and inclusion of the wider migratory landscape are fundamental to the integrity of the property and reflect the ecological reality that the migration system depends upon ecological connectivity across a vast and dynamic landscape. The property retains the key ecological attributes necessary to convey its Outstanding Universal Value, including large migratory wildlife populations, extensive seasonal habitats and relatively intact migration corridors. However, at the time of inscription, the property faces significant threats, including commercial poaching and wildlife trafficking, infrastructure development, insecurity, potential extractive activities, incomplete protection and management arrangements across parts of the wider landscape, and limited institutional and financial capacity. The long-term integrity of the property will depend upon maintaining ecological connectivity, safeguarding migration corridors and seasonal habitats, and ensuring that future development does not adversely affect the ecological processes that underpin Outstanding Universal Value. Protection and management requirements The property includes two legally protected areas, Boma National Park and Badingilo National Park, which provide an important foundation for conservation. The property is managed under the authority of the Ministry of Wildlife Conservation and Tourism and benefits from a management partnership with African Parks. The Wildlife Conservation and Protected Areas Act and other relevant legislation provide the principal legal framework for conservation. The long-term conservation of the property requires a landscape-scale approach to protection and management due to the fact that the ecological processes and migration system that underpin its Outstanding Universal Value are found largely beyond the boundaries of the two national parks. Priority actions, at the time of inscription, include strengthening legal protection within the national parks and across the wider migratory landscape, completing and implementing an integrated landscape-scale land-use and management framework, strengthening consultation, engagement and partnership with Indigenous Peoples and local communities, enhancing management capacity and infrastructure, maintaining ecological connectivity, conserving migration corridors and seasonal habitats, and strengthening governance arrangements for areas outside the existing protected areas. Effective conservation will require sustained investment in law enforcement, ecological monitoring, research, community engagement and institutional capacity, together with measures to address commercial wildlife exploitation, infrastructure development and other pressures affecting the property. The meaningful participation of Indigenous Peoples and local communities in governance, planning and management processes, including through Free, Prior and Informed Consent, will be essential to the long-term conservation of the property's Outstanding Universal Value.

Natural Criteria: n7, n9, n10

Name: Village of Sidi Bou Saïd

Short Description: The property is a picturesque village perched on a promontory overlooking the Mediterranean Sea, harmoniously integrated into the cliff topography. It developed around the tomb of a Sufi master and saint, known as Sidi Bou Saïd, who lived in the 12th-13th centuries. Through its architectural fabric and urban planning in symbiosis with the natural environment, its recognisable aesthetic created by emblematic colours, and a mystic aura associated with the Sufi spirituality that permeates the site, the property brings together geomorphology, architecture, and spirituality. It has long inspired artists and continues to attract visitors seeking spiritual serenity.

Description: The property is a picturesque village perched on a promontory overlooking the Mediterranean Sea, harmoniously integrated into the cliff topography. It developed around the tomb of a Sufi master and saint, known as Sidi Bou Saïd, who lived in the 12th-13th centuries. Through its architectural fabric and urban planning in symbiosis with the natural environment, its recognisable aesthetic created by emblematic colours, and a mystic aura associated with the Sufi spirituality that permeates the site, the property brings together geomorphology, architecture, and spirituality. It has long inspired artists and continues to attract visitors seeking spiritual serenity.

Justification: Brief synthesis The Village of Sidi Bou Saïd is located on top of a hill overlooking the Mediterranean Sea, in northern Tunisia. It developed as a sanctuary-village as a result of a process of aggregation around the mausoleum of a Sufi saint – Abou Saïd Khalaf Ibn Yahya El Tamimi El Beji, known as Sidi Bou Saïd – supported by successive ruling dynasties, which, from the 16th century onwards, fostered the sacralisation of the place by associating their political legitimacy with the baraka (blessing) of the saint. The Husainid beys (18th-20th century) consolidated this dynamic by building holiday residences in Sidi Bou Saïd and turning it into an elite resort. The property embodies the encounter between the spiritual power of the saint and the temporal political power. With the religious complex of Sidi Bou Saïd at its heart, the village reflects the traditional Arab-Islamic urban planning around a central place, enriched by the 19th-20th century urban-type residential architecture of the notables. Criterion (iii): The Village of Sidi Bou Saïd represents an exceptional testimony to the tradition of village foundations based on a symbiotic relationship formed between the spiritual authority of a saint and the temporal power of a ruling dynasty. It exemplifies in an exceptional way the phenomenon of sanctuary-villages, fundamental to the social and political history of the Maghreb, that developed as a result of a saint’s prestige which provided religious legitimacy to the sovereign, and the sovereign’s patronage which, in return, ensured the perpetuation and prosperity of the saint's sanctuary and village. Integrity The property includes the entire historic village of Sidi Bou Saïd, within its 1915 boundaries, excluding a few later buildings which break with the traditional architectural style of the place. The urban morphology and the fabric of the village have been well preserved, and the landscape setting remains largely unaltered, except for the introduction of a marina below the southern slope of the promontory. Other limited instances in which the integrity of the property has been compromised and visual aspects of the site negatively affected are mostly reversible. The site suffers dangerously from instability related to its geological nature and environmental factors. Developmental pressures are largely under control, but excessive tourism is a major concern that requires strategic reorganisation, as it shows to negatively affect the character of the property. At present, despite changes in the socio-cultural and economic context of the site, the vivacity of Sufi spiritual practices persists. Authenticity The property has maintained its morphological coherence and its urban fabric has remained largely unchanged, owing to the 1915 Beylical decree, which helped preserve the village and its historical density. Land division occurred sporadically. The construction of the marina at the southern foot of the promontory modified to a small degree the landscape setting of the property. The mystical practices associated with Sufism remain active and the places of religious practices have mostly retained their original function. The identity of the village that has shaped its history and culture has been maintained, though it faces increasing threats posed by tourism. The related economic dynamics have already led to some changes in the use of residences within the village. Protection and management requirements The property is protected by the Beylical decree of 1915 and the decree 85-1246 of 1985, which provide strong controls against the changes to the spatial organisation of the village, as well as to the fabric and aesthetic of its built environment. The National Institute of Heritage under the Ministry of Cultural Affairs oversees the protection of the property through the Archaeological, Historical and Traditional Arts Heritage Code of 1994. The Institute is also the central body responsible for the management and conservation of the site. The Urban Development Plan for the municipality of Sidi Bou Saïd regulates land uses while incorporating provisions for the protection of heritage, in line with the Territorial and Urban Planning Code of 1994. The management plan has been prepared for a pilot phase (until 2027) and will be further developed.

Cultural Criteria: c3

Name: Amazonia Theaters

Short Description: The property consists of two component parts: The Theatro da Paz and the Praça da República in Belém, and the Teatro Amazonas and the Largo de São Sebastião in Manaus. These were built in the States of Pará and Amazonas in Brazil during the Amazonian ‘Golden Age’ as a result of the economic peak of the Rubber Cycle between 1879 and 1912. Inspired by French and European architecture and decorated with motifs evoking the Amazon, these ensembles were designed as symbols of political and urban ambition. Inaugurated in 1878 and 1889, the Theatro da Paz and the Praça da República asserted the strategic role of the city of Belém as a port and State capital and celebrated the Brazilian Republic, while the Teatro Amazonas, inaugurated in 1896, was part of the large-scale urban development of Manaus during the rubber boom and, along with the Largo de São Sebastião, expressed the wealth and prestige of the future capital of the Amazon.

Name: The Medinas of the Historic Sultanates of the Comoros

Short Description: The serial property is composed of six historic towns which developed from urban nuclei that emerged around at least the 11th century and evolved into city-states around the 14th-15th century. They eventually became the principal urban centres of the sultanates established on the islands of the archipelago of Comoros. With a common hierarchical system of social organisation, based on matrilineal and matrilocal customs, age-group systems, and patrilineal Islamic traditions still alive today, the property showcases insular urban forms and architectural expressions that resulted from cultural exchanges related to migration and Indian Ocean trade networks, embedded in the local social, geographical, and environmental context.

Description: The serial property is composed of six historic towns which developed from urban nuclei that emerged around at least the 11th century and evolved into city-states around the 14th-15th century. They eventually became the principal urban centres of the sultanates established on the islands of the archipelago of Comoros. With a common hierarchical system of social organisation, based on matrilineal and matrilocal customs, age-group systems, and patrilineal Islamic traditions still alive today, the property showcases insular urban forms and architectural expressions that resulted from cultural exchanges related to migration and Indian Ocean trade networks, embedded in the local social, geographical, and environmental context.

Justification: Brief synthesis The serial property comprises the best-preserved parts of six historic cities located on the islands of Ngazidja and Ndzuwani in the Comoros. They developed from urban nuclei that emerged around at least the 11th century and evolved into city-states around the 14th-15th century, becoming eventually the principal urban centres of the sultanates established in the archipelago of Comoros within the framework of the formation of a Muslim elite linked to the Swahili world. This heritage ensemble, encompassing urban, architectural, and intangible elements, reflects the richness and specificity of Swahili cultural tradition within the Comorian island context. The former sultanic medinas have preserved their old urban morphology and fabric, and an exceptional set of traditions and social practices still alive today. Compact fabrics, with centrally organised palaces and public squares (bangwe, mpangahari), stone houses and defensive structures, the medinas showcase insular urban forms and architectural expressions that resulted from cultural exchanges related to migration and Indian Ocean trade networks, while displaying a spatial logic dictated by a hierarchical system of social organisation based on matrilineal and matrilocal customs, age-group systems, and patrilineal Islamic traditions. The Comorian historic cities, though founded upon the same fundamental cultural and social basis, evolved along distinct trajectories shaped by their geographic, political, social and historical contexts. Criterion (iii): The Medinas of the Historic Sultanates of the Comoros provide an exceptional testimony to the living cultural traditions and social practices of the Comorian archipelago, which, due to its location and complex history, has become a crossroads for peoples of different origins, between Africa, the Arab world, and Europe, connected by the Indian Ocean. The hierarchical social structures of the Comorian society, based on a synthesis of matrilineal and matrilocal customs, age-group system, and patrilineal Islamic traditions, are reflected in the urban organisation of the medinas, which serve as a setting for social life and celebrations that mark the stages of life of men and women, and which in turn give the tangible heritage its meaning. Criterion (iv): The Medinas of the Historic Sultanates of the Comoros constitute a constellation of distinctive responses in architecture and landscape-making that collectively demonstrate the originality of Comorian urban traditions that adapted Arab-Shirazi influences to the local geographic context and combined them with African social structures and models of communal living. Through complementary responses in architecture, artistry, defensive systems, and landscape-making, created within a shared cultural matrix, the component parts showcase the origins and evolution of urbanism in the Comoros, linked to the arrival of Islam, which marked a significant cultural phase in the history of the Indian Ocean region, and illustrates a historical period that witnessed the development of interaction and exchanges between African cultures, the Arab-Muslim world, and various European powers, and the progressive integration of the region into the global maritime context. Integrity While the Comorian medinas of the series share historical and socio-cultural foundations that structure them, the component parts showcase the diversity of architectural, artistic, and planning responses. Each contributes individually to the series through the varying intensities and modalities of external exchanges which, combined with adaptations to specific geographical and insular contexts, generated distinct urban forms and stylistic identities. The component parts include the best-preserved, but sufficiently large, sections of each medina, with the remaining intra-muros areas and some immediate setting comprised within the buffer zones. The serial property retains high integrity in terms of urban morphology, and the system of religious and socio-cultural spaces and centres. However, the oldest built structures (palaces, city walls, historic mosques) are highly vulnerable, with several cases in serious disrepair. The visual interconnections between the cities and the key elements of their natural environment (volcanos, hills, sea), the geographic setting and the maritime connection to the cities are elements that are functionally important as a support to the protection of the property. Authenticity The urban morphology and the spirit of the medinas remain strong in all six component parts, and the authenticity of their use and function is also very high. However, the authenticity of the material fabric of the historic cities has been partly compromised, particularly where concrete reconstructions have been carried out. The gradual loss of traditional skills and massive replacement of materials represent serious threats to the authenticity of the serial property. Historically, the intra-muros sections of the medinas have not been drastically transformed or remodelled, but areas outside the city walls were affected in the modern times. The relationship of the urban centres with the sea is not fully preserved today due to modern developments. Moreover, none of the medinas maintained the maritime commercial context that characterised them during the sultanate era. The intangible heritage still structures the historic cities and gives meaning to the public and private spaces within the medinas. The customary system makes them living spaces of civic and moral education. Protection and management requirements The serial property is protected by Law No. 20-033/AU of 2020 on the Protection of Cultural and Natural Heritage in the Union of the Comoros, promulgated by Presidential Decree no. 21-013/PR. The development within the component parts is regulated by the Urban Planning and Housing Code of 1986, revised in 2011 by Law no. 11-026 on Urban Planning and Construction in the Union of the Comoros. Both legislations need to be supplemented with regulatory texts, which are under preparation. The Framework Law of the Environment no. 94-018, amended in 1995, regulates the landscape environment. Customary, religious, and traditional laws also apply in all component parts. The legislative basis for the creation of a national inventory has been instituted by the establishment of the National Commission for the Protection of Cultural Heritage (CNPPC), responsible for the definition, implementation, and monitoring of the heritage protection policy. This will allow for the registration or listing of the component parts and their enhanced protection at the highest national level, which is yet to be achieved. The National Office for the Valorisation of Heritage (ONVP) is in charge of the mobilisation of funding for the management, valorisation, and tourism promotion. Urban planning instruments (such as Territorial Development Plans (SAT) or Urban Development Plans (PDU)) are either not yet in place or are currently being developed. Four key ministries are involved in the different aspects of management of the serial property: the Ministry of Youth, Employment, Labour, Sports, Arts, and Culture (preservation of historical monuments and sites, their conservation and development); the Ministry of National Education, Teaching, Scientific Research, Training and Professional Integration (scientific research and training); the Ministry of the Environment, responsible for Tourism; and the Ministry of Regional Planning, Urban Development, responsible for Land Affairs and Land Transport. The National Centre for Documentation and Scientific Research (CNDRS), a public scientific and cultural institution, coordinates activities across different stakeholders. The six component parts administratively fall under six municipalities in four prefectures, whose mandate over the serial property is however limited since most of the land is privately owned or is part of the municipal estate. The traditional management system is primarily implemented through the Village Development Committees. The civil society organisations play an active role in the implementation of public policies at the local level and are formally integrated into the management system through the appointment of site managers from among their members. The management plan with an action plan covering the period 2025-2034 is divided into two phases and is being implemented.

Cultural Criteria: c3, c4

text:
Name: Royal Capetian Fortresses of Languedoc

Short Description: The serial property comprises eight fortified sites – Castle and ramparts of Carcassonne and the fortresses of Aguilar, Lastours, Montségur, Peyrepertuse, Puilaurens, Quéribus, and Termes – representing a core part of the Capetian defensive system established in the 13th–14th centuries following the Albigensian Crusade. Built on rugged rocky ridges in strategically significant locations, these fortifications formed the backbone of the newly created seneschalty of Carcassonne, asserting the authority of the seneschal over the former territories of independent feudal lineages. Together, they illustrate the political, military and territorial consolidation of the Capetian Crown in Languedoc through ostentatious architecture adapted to dramatic topography.

Built on rugged rocky ridges in strategically significant locations, these fortifications formed the backbone of the newly created seneschalty of Carcassonne, asserting the authority of the seneschal over the former territories of independent feudal lineages. Together, they illustrate the political, military and territorial consolidation of the Capetian Crown in Languedoc through ostentatious architecture adapted to dramatic topography.

Justification: Brief synthesis The regional defensive fortification system established by the Capetian kings in the 13th-14th centuries in the former seneschalty of Carcassonne, in the Occitanie region, consisted of twenty-two fortresses built to protect the seneschal’s headquarters at Carcassonne, secure newly annexed lands, monitor the border with the Kingdom of Aragon, safeguard economic resources and control key communication routes, as well as assert royal power in the region through monumental architecture. This serial property, composed of eight component parts, comprises a representative sample of this system and includes the Carcassonne Castle with its double concentric ramparts, which served as the administrative and military centre of the seneschalty, as well as an ensemble of watchmen fortresses built in a relatively short span of time under royal supervision in a rugged topography. The system of the fortresses of the seneschalty of Carcassonne, stylistically consistent, was designed based on the Capetian military architecture models, developed for the plains of Ile-de-France and adapted to the rocky topography of the Montagne Noire and the Pyrenean foothills. The serial property represents a compelling example of this defensive architecture, which served as a political tool to project the growing, centralised and divinely sanctioned power of the French monarchy, part of a larger movement towards assertion of sovereign powers that marked 13th-century Europe. Criterion (iv): A centrally commanded territorial defensive ensemble with shared architectural language and military functions, The System of Fortresses of the Seneschalty of Carcassonne is an exceptional example of the highly standardised Capetian military architecture carefully adapted to the difficult topography of the territory in which it was implanted. As the only coherent fortification system built by the Capetian kings, it testifies to the strengthening and considerable expansion of the Capetian dynasty power in France in the 13th-14th centuries, marking the political shift from feudal fragmentation to the emergence of a strong centralised monarchy. Integrity The serial property includes a coherent and well-preserved selection of mountain fortresses and their administrative centre (Carcassonne Castle) which are representative of the fortification system of the seneschalty of Carcassonne. The component parts fit together in a clear manner, and each contributes individually to the series through specific designs and adaptations, demonstrating diversity of technical solutions in architectural landscape integration. All the mountain fortresses (component parts 02 to 08) are ruined to a different degree, which is a result of the historical process. They have not undergone major transformations that would significantly alter their structures. The Castle of Carcassonne and its ramparts (component part 01) display major reconstructions undertaken in the 19th century. The landscape setting of the watchmen fortresses (component parts 02 to 08) has been well preserved; their strategic location on hills that provided visibility over vast territories is still perfectly evident. In the case of the Castle of Carcassonne and its ramparts (component part 01), the rural landscape persists in places, but residential buildings and industrial settlements have also developed in the immediate vicinity. The integrity of the serial property is not threatened by immediate risks. Authenticity The component parts display truthfully the defining vocabulary of Capetian military architecture, while their placement demonstrates its adaptability to challenging topography. Scientific research in recent years has clarified the distinction between the 13th- and 14th-century sections and the 19th-century sections of the Castle of Carcassonne and its ramparts (component part 01). There is now sufficient evidence to confirm that the majority of the structures of this component part date back to the fortifications built by the Capetian kings to defend the seneschalty. Tourism infrastructure created at the site has nonetheless had an impact on the perception of the historic fabric. The other fortresses (component parts 02 to 08) maintain their original designs while displaying imposing ruins that still convey the nature and qualities of the 13th-14th century Capetian military architecture. Located in rugged terrain in rural landscapes, they attract slow and contemplative tourism. Protection and management requirements All component parts are legally protected at the highest level as historic monuments, together with their immediate surroundings, which also benefit from protection as registered or listed natural sites. Protection of the buffer zones in ensured through a mix of designations under the Heritage Code and the Environmental Code. At the local level, several planification tools are in place to control development including one Local Urban Development Plan (PLU), two Intermunicipal Local Urban Development Plans (PLUi), and two Territorial Coherence Schemes (SCoT). Landscape Influence Areas (AIP) have been established for each component part to control major infrastructural projects that may negatively affect the property. The governance system of the serial property includes the Committee of the Property as the decision-making body and the Permanent Technical Committee, Technical Management Commissions, Scientific Committee, and the World Heritage Mission Association (AMPM), responsible for operationalisation. The AMPM plays a coordinating role and will ultimately become the definitive management body of the serial property. The management plan is in place and is being implemented.

Cultural Criteria: c4

Name: The wider area of Mount Olympus

Short Description: Mount Olympus is situated in northern Greece and is the highest mountain in the country. Its microclimate, resulting from its proximity to the sea and abrupt elevation, produces a remarkable diversity in terrain, climate, and vegetation. In this landscape, the ancient Greeks situated the abode of their Twelve Olympian Gods, with Zeus as their sovereign, as well as the Muses and Graces. Through the writings of Hesiod and Homer, Mount Olympus became a central point of reference for Greek mythology throughout the Greek and Roman worlds, rendering Mount Olympus an enduring emblem of Greek civilisation. The serial property features striking landforms, including glacial cirques, limestone cliffs, karstic sinkholes, and olistolith fields, while sharp ridges like the Mytikas-Stefani complex and deep gorges such as the Enipeas illustrate ongoing neotectonic activity. Mount Olympus has served as a glacial refugium for forest species and is also a Mediterranean plant biodiversity and endemism hotspot.

text:
Name: Ancient Capitals of Asuka and Fujiwara

Short Description: Located in the southern part of the Nara Basin, Asuka and Fujiwara were the two ancient capitals of the Japanese archipelago that marked the establishment of a centralised state system modelled after the Chinese codified law known as ritsuryō. Nineteen component parts, comprising palaces/government offices, Buddhist temples and mounded tombs, contain archaeological evidence of the Asuka Capital (588-694 CE) and the Fujiwara Capital (694-710 CE). The Asuka capital was established at the site of the Asuka-dera Temple, the first Buddhist temple in Japan. Together, the sites illustrate the introduction and consolidation of key elements of early centralized governance and influenced the later Japanese capitals of Nara and Kyoto.

Description: Located in the southern part of the Nara Basin, Asuka and Fujiwara were the two ancient capitals of the Japanese archipelago that marked the establishment of a centralised state system modelled after the Chinese codified law known as ritsuryō. Nineteen component parts, comprising palaces/government offices, Buddhist temples and mounded tombs, contain archaeological evidence of the Asuka Capital (588-694 CE) and the Fujiwara Capital (694-710 CE). The Asuka capital was established at the site of the Asuka-dera Temple, the first Buddhist temple in Japan. Together, the sites illustrate the introduction and consolidation of key elements of early centralized governance and influenced the later Japanese capitals of Nara and Kyoto.

Justification: Brief synthesis The Ancient Capitals of Asuka and Fujiwara are a serial property of nineteen component parts that are associated with two consecutive early capitals on the Japanese archipelago established through interchanges with kingdoms in China and the Korean Peninsula. Located in the Nara Basin, these sites attest to the formative processes of the emergence and establishment of centralised state systems in East Asia, modelled on the Chinese ritsuryo system. The capitals of Asuka and Fujiwara influenced the construction and evolution of subsequent capitals in Japan, including the Nara Capital in the 8th century and the Heian Capital in Kyoto in the 9th century. The layout, design, technology, and planning of the two capitals were a result of a fusion between local traditions and adoption of culture and technology from other East Asian powers. The nineteen component parts have been selected to represent three tangible and spatial dimensions of these capitals: palace/government office sites, Buddhist temple sites, and mounded tombs. The sites associated with the Asuka capital (588-694 CE) reflect the initial stages of the implementation of the centralised state and feature the concentration of political power in the palace and the gradual addition of governing facilities. The Asuka-dera Temple (component part 005) was the first Buddhist temple in the Japanese archipelago and marks the introduction of Buddhism. Private temples and new types of mounded tombs began to appear in areas under the influence of powerful clans. The sites of the subsequent capital at Fujiwara (694-710 CE) represent the completion of this stage of central power development. The palace, including government offices, was positioned at the centre of the capital, with state temples and the systematic arrangement of tombs. Criterion (ii): The layout, design, technology, and planning of the palace/government office sites, Buddhist temple sites and mounded tombs of the Ancient Capitals of Asuka and Fujiwara represent an important interchange of human values with contemporary power centres in China and the Korean Peninsula, and the introduction of Buddhism to Japan. These early capitals exerted profound influences on the construction and evolution of capitals on the Japanese archipelago from the 8th century onwards. Criterion (iii): The sites associated with the Ancient Capitals of Asuka and Fujiwara form an important testimony to the cultural tradition of the formative processes of ancient capitals in East Asia based on centralised state systems through their locations, spatial layout and relationships and composition. Integrity The nineteen component parts that comprise the Ancient Capitals of Asuka and Fujiwara contain the necessary attributes needed to represent the formation and characteristics of these early centralised state systems in the Japanese archipelago. Most of the archaeological remains are located below the ground surface. They have been well-researched and are maintained in a stable condition. The boundaries are adequate, and the single encompassing buffer zone provides an added layer of protection. Key pressures are actively managed. Authenticity The attributes of Outstanding Universal Value are archaeological sites that were covered below the ground surface after the Ancient Capitals of Asuka and Fujiwara were abandoned. Since that time, the land has been used for agriculture and the archaeological remains have a good state of conservation. The evidence of the spatial layout and configuration of the two ancient capitals is confirmed by archaeological excavations and historical literature. The sites are re-buried following archaeological excavations and above-ground representations using non-destructive methods and materials have been established to enable visualisation and interpretation. Protection and management requirements The Ancient Capitals of Asuka and Fujiwara are protected by law at the national and local levels. The component parts are protected either as Historic Site, Special Historic Site, or Place of Scenic Beauty under the Law for the Protection of Cultural Properties; or as Imperial Mausoleum under the National Property Act. Changes or developments within these areas are strictly regulated. Protection of the buffer zone is based on the Act on Special Measures Concerning the Preservation of Historic Landscape in Ancient Capitals and the Act on Special Measures Concerning the Preservation of Historic Landscape and Improvement of Living Environment in Asuka Village. There are controls on the alteration of landforms, and on the height, colour, and design of new structures. The Scenic Zone is designated by the local government ordinance under the City Planning Act to ensure conservation of the surrounding environment. Parts of the buffer zone are directly managed by the national government as a national government park. Within the buffer zone, underground archaeological remains are protected under the Law for the Protection of Cultural Properties as “Land Known to Contain Buried Cultural Properties”. There is a Comprehensive Preservation and Management Plan for the serial property and buffer zone. The Asuka-Fujiwara World Heritage Council provides a coordinated management mechanism, consisting of the Nara Prefecture, Kashihara City, Sakurai City, and Asuka Village. Each component part has an individual management plan. The component parts and buffer zone are subject to systematic monitoring and daily maintenance.

Cultural Criteria: c2, c3

text:
Name: Rock Mosques and Associated Sacred Sites of Mangystau

Short Description: The serial property, located on the Mangystau Peninsula bordering the Caspian Sea, consists of five sacred sites carved into the rock along with adjacent extensive burial grounds. Beket-Ata, Shopan-Ata, Karaman-Ata, Shakpak-Ata and Sultan-Epe, each associated with a Sufi master, date from the 12th to the 18th centuries. The complexes, known locally as “underground mosques”, are a particular type of structure created in natural caves, carved into steep rocks or dug into the ground in the semi-desert landscape. Originating in the nomadic environment of the Mangystau and Ustyurt plateaus, the component parts represent a culture that is the result of the evolution of sacred practices in which Islamic Sufi spirituality organically continued and transformed more ancient practices related to ancestor worship, the sacredness of the landscape and the role of spiritual leaders. They have been important pilgrimage destinations throughout the centuries. The rock-carved sacred sites range from smaller structures to more complex spaces. They have different architectural layouts and organisation, including prayer halls, mihrabs, rooms for contemplation and self-reflection, multifunctional spaces and tombs of saints. The complexes comprise courtyards, water sources, sacred trees, paths and cemeteries, the latter dating from the 10th to the 20th centuries.

Name: Okefenokee National Wildlife Refuge

Short Description: The property, located in southeastern Georgia and northeastern Florida, protects the Okefenokee Swamp, the largest lowland freshwater peatland in the subtropical zone worldwide and one of the largest and most intact ecosystems within the North American Coastal Plain global biodiversity hotspot. The property comprises a diverse mosaic of wetlands, savannas, and forests shaped by the ongoing interaction of water, fire, vegetation, and wildlife, with alternating fire and rainfall processes driving peat formation, vegetation structure, and biodiversity. The site also contains significant areas of endangered Longleaf Pine (Pinus palustris) savanna, of which less than 3% remains, supporting high concentrations of plant species endemic to the region. Its extensive peat deposits provide an important archive of palaeo-environmental history and critical carbon storage. The property supports exceptional biodiversity, including at least 856 plant species, 48 mammal species, 238 bird species, 39 fish species, and 90 reptile and amphibian species, and provides important habitat for migratory birds, threatened species, and a significant population of American alligators.

Description: The property, located in southeastern Georgia and northeastern Florida, protects the Okefenokee Swamp, the largest lowland freshwater peatland in the subtropical zone worldwide and one of the largest and most intact ecosystems within the North American Coastal Plain global biodiversity hotspot. The property comprises a diverse mosaic of wetlands, savannas, and forests shaped by the ongoing interaction of water, fire, vegetation, and wildlife, with alternating fire and rainfall processes driving peat formation, vegetation structure, and biodiversity. The site also contains significant areas of endangered Longleaf Pine (Pinus palustris) savanna, of which less than 3% remains, supporting high concentrations of plant species endemic to the region. Its extensive peat deposits provide an important archive of palaeo-environmental history and critical carbon storage. The property supports exceptional biodiversity, including at least 856 plant species, 48 mammal species, 238 bird species, 39 fish species, and 90 reptile and amphibian species, and provides important habitat for migratory birds, threatened species, and a significant population of American alligators.

Justification: Brief synthesis Located primarily in the southeast of the State of Georgia and the northeast of the State of Florida, the Okefenokee National Wildlife Refuge (ONWR) protects the spectacular Okefenokee Swamp, a vast and globally unique subtropical peatland. The ONWR is situated in an area of great historical, cultural, and spiritual significance for the Muscogee (Creek) Nation, among other Indigenous Peoples, who inhabited the area before colonization and their forced removal. The Okefenokee Swamp is considered the largest lowland freshwater peatland in the subtropical zone worldwide and is one of the largest and most intact remaining ecosystems within the North American Coastal Plain (NACP) global biodiversity hotspot. The interplay between the pine savannas and wetlands of the Okefenokee Swamp weaves together exceptional hydrologic, pyrogenic, and vegetation processes with complex faunal interactions. The ONWR also protects significant areas of Longleaf Pine (Pinus palustris) savanna, an endangered ecosystem found only in the southeastern United States of America, and of which less than 3% remains. The extensive and intact peat layers in the ONWR also provide an irreplaceable archive of local, regional and global palaeo-environmental history, as well as critical carbon storage. Criterion (ix): The ONWR encompasses a highly diverse mosaic of wetlands, savannas, and forest ecosystems characterized by exceptional and ongoing interactions between water, fire, flora, and fauna. The cycle of alternating fire and rainfall processes drive peat formation, shape vegetation structure, and support high levels of biodiversity. It is one of the largest wetland complexes in North America, and is likely the world’s largest and most intact lowland freshwater (primarily precipitation-fed) peatland in the subtropical zone. The property hosts a significant portion (approximately 11,200 hectares) of Longleaf Pine (Pinus palustris) savanna, found only in the southeastern United States of America, and of which only approximately 3% remains. These pine savannas form a complete ecosystem and support a high concentration of plant species endemic to the NACP. Criterion (x): The unique ecosystem dynamics and location of the ONWR contribute to its high biodiversity values and is representativeness of the North American Coastal Plain (NACP) global biodiversity hotspot, including high percentages of regionally endemic species. The ONWR is home to at least 856 species of plants, 48 species of mammals, 238 species of birds, 39 species of fish, 90 species of reptiles and amphibians, and a large number of invertebrates. The herpetofauna of the ONWR is particularly high for a temperate or subtropical ecosystem, and includes an important population of American alligators, which act as the keystone predator and landscape architect. The property is an important refuge and breeding ground for migratory birds. The ONWR acts as a refuge for many threatened species, primarily tree species, reptiles, and birds. Integrity The ONWR is of adequate size to ensure the complete representation of its key values and ecological processes, including the interaction of fire and hydrology, which are critical to maintaining the property’s exceptional values. Its size, relative inaccessibility, and long-standing protection under the National Wilderness Preservation System, provides the property with very high degree of ecological integrity. While the ONWR suffered adverse effects from unsuccessful drainage attempts and logging operations predating the establishment of the ONWR, these impacts were followed by nearly a century of natural recovery and active restoration, with minimal current impacts. While the property does not have a formal buffer zone, a functional combination of measures in the immediate surroundings, including the presence of neighbouring protected areas, collaborative efforts to create a fire-resistant buffer area surrounding the ONWR, and continued land acquisition along the ONWR’s border in partnership with non-profit organizations, supports its conservation objectives. The main threats to the property include impacts of climate change on the presence and severity of fires and changes in the hydrological regime, and industrial and development pressures from outside the ONWR, particularly, mining interests, water management from commercial forestry, and diverse impacts from urbanization in the broader area. Protection and management requirements The ONWR was established in 1937 by Executive Order, and 87% of it was classified as a National Wilderness Area in 1974 under the Wilderness Act by Congress and designated as part of the National Wilderness Preservation System, thus providing for strict protection. The ONWR is managed by the United States Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS), in partnership with private enterprises that provide visitor services. Management is guided by a 15-year Comprehensive Conservation Plan (CCP) to maintain its ecological integrity and manage visitation, with an update expected at the time of inscription. The property is effectively protected through robust federal legislation at the time of nomination, including the National Environmental Policy Act (1970), Endangered Species Act (1973), Fish and Wildlife Act (1959), Clean Water Act (1977), Archaeological Resources Protection Act (1979), and Executive Order 13007 Indian Sacred Sites (1996), among others. Any reforms to the applicable legislation and the CCP need to ensure adequate protection for the attributes sustaining the Outstanding Universal Value of the property. With the ONWR being of great historical, cultural, and spiritual significance for the Muscogee (Creek) Nation, among other Indigenous Peoples, collaboration has grown between the ONWR management authorities and the Muscogee (Creek) Nation in the years leading up to the nomination. The Muscogee (Creek) Nation has identified 74 ancestral burial mounds within the ONWR and aim to have the area declared Traditional Cultural Property under the National Historic Preservation Act of 1966. The Muscogee (Creek) Nation considers it indispensable that cultural heritage values of the ONWR be recognized and appropriately protected alongside its natural values. It is thus important to reflect these values in the management framework of the property. The collection, storage, and disclosure of specific information and locations of sacred sites within the ONWR should be treated with sensitivity and led by the Indigenous Peoples concerned.

Natural Criteria: n9, n10

Name: The Roças of Sao Tome and Principe: Colonial Agricultural System and Forced Migration

Short Description: The serial property comprises six geographically separate roças (Portuguese colonial agricultural plantations) located on the islands of Sao Tome and Principe: Monte Café, Agua Izé, Diogo Vaz, Sao Joao, Sundy, and Belo Monte. Together, they represent a planned colonial plantation system dedicated primarily to coffee and cocoa production, combining agricultural land, industrial infrastructure, residential areas, and social facilities within highly structured spatial layouts. The property illustrates the operation of a large-scale colonial agro-industrial system, based on forced migration and labour, from the late 19th century through the mid-20th century, to sustain global commodity production after the abolition of slavery.

text:
Name: Wadi Wurayah

Short Description: The property is located entirely within the Hajar mountain range in the Emirate of Fujairah. Geologically, the Hajar Mountains represent extensive and well-preserved exposures of ophiolite sequences, formed during Late Cretaceous tectonic processes. Ecologically, the property is situated within the Al Hajar Foothill Xeric Woodlands and Shrublands, recognised for its ecological distinctiveness, high species richness, and significant levels of endemism. Wadi Wurayah hosts 1,099 recorded species (883 fauna and 216 flora), including at least ten globally threatened species. These represent approximately half of the terrestrial mammal species and nearly half of the terrestrial reptile species recorded in the country.

Name: Murujuga Cultural Landscape

Short Description: Murujuga is a deeply storied land and seascape located in northwest Australia. It encompasses the Burrup Peninsula, the Dampier Archipelago, surrounding marine areas and the submerged landscape. Murujuga is shaped by the Lore — rules and narratives put in place to create the Country — and the enduring presence of the Ngarda-Ngarli, Traditional Owners and Custodians of the site. The property holds profound cultural and spiritual significance, reflecting over 50,000 years of continuous care and management by Traditional Law that has adapted to the changing needs of Country over periods of dramatic climatic and environmental change. Murujuga is renowned for its dense concentration of archaeological and spiritual sites that reflect the interaction between people and place over thousands of generations. Its extraordinary rock art assemblage records a complex system of Lore and Traditional Law, features unique motifs and demonstrates artistic and technical mastery.
